items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items._cn_summary: Gerry Hemingway领衔的跨国组合汇集德国、瑞士、爱尔兰及美国乐手，以多件簧乐器、低音提琴、钢琴和鼓为核心，在瑞士阿尔特比隆Bau 4锯木厂改造的场地录制这张现场专辑。作品包含长达三十六分钟与二十三分钟的组曲式长篇，以及一段六分钟的双人即兴穿插其中。乐评指出，长曲融合了记谱段落与自由即兴，类似于Hemingway早年与Anthony Braxton合作的经验，以低音乐器在底层的齐奏、打击乐中融入木块作槌等手法构建叙事张力。钢琴与鼓的二重奏展现出对脉动的精准捕捉与音色配合，评论者特别强调此段的默契程度。长篇作品在固定段落之间存在松弛区间，鼓手自由挥洒的松弛风格有时被评价为力度不足。整体以学院派自由爵士为核心，融合当代作曲式的篇章结构与现场即兴呼吸，是欧洲实验爵士现场的高质量记录。

items.body: The shift from music as a way of showing off the wealth and splendour of royalty, aristocracy, or principality to music as a way of generating private profit brought with it a corresponding downsizing of the typical ensemble. Today, a few large, 100-piece orchestras still retain a precarious existence as museum acts; meanwhile, the vast majority of new music is composed and performed by individuals or small groups, with fewer ways to cut the profit pie meaning bigger slices all round (and, for many musicians, the difference between being able to eat or not). No doubt technology has played a role in this too — it’s now possible for a single individual with access to a computer to compose, record, and master a piece of music as grand in scale as anything by Mahler. Plus, isn’t it just easier to get things done when there’s only yourself to organise? Into this context step the Insub Meta Orchestra, a 50-piece ensemble with members from Switzerland, France, Belgium and Germany that operates in the fertile space between formal composition and improvisation. 32 musicians contributed to their new album “13 and 27”, and for the piece ‘13 unissons’ were split into 13 subgroups, each of which plays just one note in unison, repeated as often as they like. Most of the tones are long in duration, and the various unisons often create faint beating, resonance, or haze around a tone. Silence is used to separate out the playing into distinct moments, resulting in several sustained chords with various configurations of pitches. It’s pleasant enough, but not necessarily groundbreaking; maybe I’ve just heard too many pieces of a similar ilk. ‘27 times’ is a more complex piece. Each musician was asked to choose his or her ‘most unique, personal sound’, which they then repeated 27 times across roughly half an hour. Many of the chosen sounds turn out to be faint, dissonant, and/or quite rough in timbre, with the low volume and tentative pacing keeping things tense and muted rather than aggressive or harsh. The effect is like walking through a deserted city at night, one form morphing into another in the dark-obscured unfolding of urban topology. The repetition here is even stronger than in ‘13 unissons’, in the sense that form, pitch and duration are more closely matched between repetitions, but paradoxically this serves to underscore subtle differences in timbre, pitch, and resonance. This is certainly the more engaging and evocative piece of the pair for me. The logistical (not to mention financial) challenges of convening and organising such a large group of musicians would be enough to put many people off, but as Insub instigators Cyril Bondi and d’incise and their collaborators have discovered, it prompts new ways of thinking about how to make music together with others. From a listener’s point of view, it widens and diversifies our musical world still further. Insub Meta Orchestra Another Timbre
items._genre: experimental / contemporary classical / large ensemble improvisation / drone / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: Insub Meta Orchestra 是一支由瑞士、法国、比利时和德国音乐家组成的五十人大型乐团，横跨正式作曲与即兴演奏之间。专辑《13 and 27》收录两首作品：《13 unissons》将三十二位乐手分成十三个子组，每组演奏一个统一音高，自由重复，乐句悠长，通过不同泛音与拍频产生朦胧共鸣，但评论者认为手法并不算突破性；《27 times》则要求每位乐手选择自己最独特的声音，重复二十七次，音量低微、节奏试探，声音细碎且带轻微不协和与粗糙质感，呈现出深夜空城中形态渐变的听觉体验。在大型乐团运作日趋困难的当下，这张专辑探索了集体创作的新思维方式，为听众拓展了音乐的感知边界。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国驻肯尼亚打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的二人组Odd Okoddo，携手83岁肯尼亚传统dodo流派歌手Ogoya Nengo共同完成，是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手鼓与套鼓为嗓音搭建框架，其合成化复合节奏层层递进、微妙至极，最终与人声融为一体，使传统根源呈现出前卫质感。曲目《Bara》从廉价的重复打击乐声起，逐步叠加4/4节拍、低音与木琴音色；《Sarah》则以Ratengo的主唱配合Kacirek试探性的打击碎点，电子元素在高潮处悄然刺入。两位歌手同住一地，根源相近，演唱中你来我往，形成代际与地域的深度对话。这张作品体现了21世纪跨文化协作的可能性——传统并未被技术践踏，反而因合成器的介入而获得新生。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._genre: avant-garde / experimental / ambient / modal / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Dorothy Moskowitz联合前卫作曲家Paladino与诗人Ferrari共同创作，十一首曲目挑战了听众对西方和声进行的固有认知。音乐以钢琴为核心，辅以弦乐、木管与合成器织体，常处于失谐或异相状态，不遵循传统调性逻辑，呈现出非线性的旋律展开方式，被比作Steve Reich与Philip Glass的简约重复美学。歌词层面具有强烈的政治隐喻与时代批判，《Pale Wanderer》直指威权主义的帮凶机制，《Charlottesville》则与已故的Joe Byrd共同完成，对白人至上与排外情绪进行直接控诉，同时也有对死亡与人类处境的哲学沉思。Moskowitz的嗓音历经岁月沉淀，以戏剧化的方式承载诗化文本，钢琴既是人声延伸，也充当评论进程的希腊式合唱角色，整体音乐在框架、脉搏与不协和之间不断切换，营造出沉浸式的聆听体验。

items.excerpt: San Jacinto, up in the Montes de María on Colombia’s Caribbean side, had a dancer called Magdalena Ruiz. The gaiteros remembered her white smile and the grace in the way she moved, and how a gathering lifted the moment she arrived: the musicians, the dancers, the drinking, the young and the old. items.body: San Jacinto, up in the Montes de María on Colombia’s Caribbean side, had a dancer called Magdalena Ruiz. The gaiteros remembered her white smile and the grace in the way she moved, and how a gathering lifted the moment she arrived: the musicians, the dancers, the drinking, the young and the old. Adolfo Pacheco remembered her too: “Si no llegaba Magdalena, se enfriaba de la gaita el son”. If she failed to arrive, the gaitas went cold. “Ahora la evoco en mi cantar”, he sings, now I call her up in my song. Those gatherings take the shape of a rueda de cumbia. The musicians stand in the middle and the women dance around them, candles in hand, long skirts sweeping the ground. Caja and gaita set the pace and the circle follows. When Magdalena arrived, that circle opened for her. “Magdalena Ruiz” opens Madre Cumbia, the album Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto, Fruko and Carmelo Torres release on 20 October through the San Diego label Bad Vibes Good Friends. Ten songs, most of them from the sabanera repertoire: three by Andrés Landero, one Torres wrote himself, the rest from writers like Rafael Pérez and Betty Ochoa. Los Gaiteros have carried the gaitas of San Jacinto since the 1940s. Fruko was the bassist and producer who ran the golden era of Discos Fuentes. Carmelo Torres took the accordion straight from Andrés Landero, his teacher and the man who made cumbia sabanera. Between them they hold most of what happened to cumbia in the last eighty years, and this is the first time the three of them have been in a studio together. They recorded in Bogotá with nine musicians in the room, Rory Morison producing and Gabriel Torregrosa directing. On “Magdalena Ruiz” the melody belongs to Iván Salcedo‘s gaita corta, the short flute a San Jacinto cumbia is built on, and Carmelo Torres answers on accordion while Fruko holds the bass underneath. Behind them, caja, conga, guacharaca and maracas keep the rueda turning, and Rafael Castro sings the lead. Listen to “Magdalena Ruiz” and pre-order Madre Cumbia HERE The post Daily Discovery: Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto x Carmelo Torres x Fruko y Sus Tesos – Magdalena Ruiz appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 哥伦比亚加勒比海岸Montes de María地区的San Jacinto，是传统盖塔笛与手鼓交织的昆比亚音乐重镇。乐评聚焦专辑《Madre Cumbia》中的首支单曲《Magdalena Ruiz》，以当地舞者Magdalena Ruiz的传说开篇——她的白牙与优雅舞步令聚会升温，Adolfo Pacheco的诗句「若她未至，盖塔之音即冷」奠定了整首曲子的情感基调。专辑汇集三大哥伦比亚音乐巨匠：自1940年代延续传统的Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto、Discos Fuentes黄金期的贝斯手兼制作人Fruko、以及直接师承昆比亚教父Andrés Landero的键盘手Carmelo Torres，十首曲目多取自sabanera曲库。三人在波哥大同台录音，Rory Morison担纲制作、Rafael Castro主唱，Iván Salcedo的短盖塔笛与Torres的手风琴对答，Fruko的低音撑底，配以caja、conga、guacharaca与沙槌，再现女人手持蜡烛、长裙拂地的rueda de cumbia圆圈舞场景。

items.artist: Talking ‘Future Sounds of Jazz’ with Michael Reinboth and Michael Rütten

items.body: Words by Justin TurfordThe iconic ‘Future Sounds of Jazz’ series has reached its sixteenth volume, an extraordinary achievement considering the Munich label Compost Records’ founder and compiler Michael Reinboth pretty much unveiled the term ‘future jazz’. This epic series of jazz-meets-electronica compilations began in 1995 and I’ve been a fan since the first edition when Michael drew the dots between artists as diverse as Luke Vibert, Patrick Pulsinger, Jimi Tenor and The Mighty Bop (alongside some lesser known names). A sonic space of jazz-infused house, breakbeats, future jazz and spaced out electronic oddities, the shared aesthetic was a jazz sensibility even if the music lived in other generic boxes. Not in a jazz sense of live improvisational musicianship but certainly in the sense of freedom, vibes, experimentation. From this early outing the world has caught up with Michael’s vision, a vision in turn inspired by Detroit’s own ‘Hi-Tech Jazz’, the Underground Resistance (Galaxy 2 Galaxy) all-time classic that revealed that jazz and electronic music could thrive together.Thirty one years after kickstarting this journey, the label returns with volume 16 and it’s another Michael (Rütten) who has been invited by his old friend to co-curate, and together they've absolutely smashed it, offering possibly my favourite volume so far with a roster that includes Momoko Gill, Trinidadian Deep, Felix Laband, Emanative & Jessica Lauren and DJ Oil.Michael Rütten is himself an essential cog in spreading the gospel about future-leaning jazz, electronic music and more. His globally-syndicated Soulsearching radio show has run for decades, he’s a music journalist, DJ and producer and has promoted key independent artists in his hometown of Frankfurt. Who better to join in the dig?I asked them a few questions on the eve of the release.. Michael Reinboth JT - Firstly, thank you for such a great compilation! Is it the best one yet? For my tastes it definitely is.Michael Reinboth - Many thanks for the compliments. Michael Rütten - Wow, that‘s a great compliment, thank you!JT - You’ve both been friends for so long and you’ve both curated many compilations but is this the first time you have compiled a record together?Michael Reinboth - Yes indeed, we’ve known each other since the beginning of Compost, and have a a genuine shared sense of taste, a journey through time.  After Vol. 15, I had a few good tracks up my sleeve but somehow not enough to fill a 3-LP / 2-CD set. That’s when Michael Rütten came along at just the right time. He had so many great suggestions that I was quite—and extremely—positively surprised, and I motivated myself to go into seclusion once again. Ha, I then found some rough FSOJ track listings on my old computer, gave them another listen, and sent my (old) ideas to Michael. Well, Michael Rütten really stepped up his game, so we currently have over 50 great tracks on our list and are already planning the next Vol. 17 for 2027.And we've decided to go on tour together and play this music in clubs, that is, to DJ. It's been a while since we've done that, and we think it's about time. Well, we're pretty good at it. After all, we have 40 years of experience.Michael Rütten - Yeah, and it happened almost by coincidence as we were talking on the phone earlier this year about potential compilations on Compost Records in the near future generally. I was relistening to some of the last ‘Future Sounds Of Jazz’ editions, especially Vol. 13 which Michael compiled on his own, for me one of the best ones, speaking about the selection, the flow, the feeling. All making sense. Also, I am thinking about a follow up of  ‘Soulsearching’ as it’s been quite a while. We speak on a regular basis about music, life, and what’s going on in the world of music and Compost Records. A new chapter of ‘Future Sounds Of Jazz’ has been ‘in the air’ since a couple of years, as not only there are so many new brilliant artists and tracks floating around that match with the idea of the series but also a new generation of young people discovering and appreciating this special sound of no boundaries, an open minded blend of jazz and electronics. I do feel and recognize this through my radio shows and DJ sets. So, as Michael mentioned that he could only think of two people - apart from himself - who could compile a FSOJ - one of them was me - we quite spontaneously decided to do the next edition together. Overnight we had a list of more than 50 tracks and started to sort (them) out. Which has been great fun! And apart from our dear friendship and shared love for good music I really do appreciate Michael’s attitude of ‘let’s do this’ and his open mind. And trust. As I do like his way of DJing ever since. Happy that someone just recently described us as pioneers of the DJ culture, instead of speaking of veterans ; ) We are still doing it out of pure passion. Neverending. So I am very much looking forward to travelling and sharing the decks again with Michael, spreading the music we love. Making people dance to timeless tunes of past, present, future via quite spontaneous DJ sets. No prepared set lists, always inspiring, always great fun also! JT - How did you approach the shared responsibility? Were there tracks that you had to fight over to be included or was it a relaxed process? Did you have fun?Michael Reinboth - First of all, it was a pleasure to hear each other's suggestions, it's always enriching. Then we basically gave the tracks grades, on a scale of one to three. No arguments at all. We were pretty much in complete agreement.Michael Rütten - Exciting, relaxed, open minded. Always enriching to hear each other’s new discoveries. And rediscoveries, tunes, that go a long way back and feel just right in the here and now. As we are both connected with so many artists of different genres from around the world who sent their music in and checking what’s going on daily or even 24/7 ... we both can’t just listen to everything. But tell each other about exciting new stuff. And I think it‘s a premiere that a fully analogue recorded jazz song made it onto Future Sounds Of Jazz - Brittany Davis’ ‘Sun & Moon’. Thanks to Michael’s open minded flexibility he instantly said yes to my idea. Oh, and no fights, never. FUN! JT - When you started out with the idea of ‘Future Jazz’ 31 years ago (!), there were a lot less artists operating in that way but there seems to be a galaxy full of them now. Compost and the Future Jazz compilations have undoubtedly been leaders in the development and widespread awareness of the ‘scene’ - do you recognise that yourself and have a sense of pride in your essential contribution?Michael Reinboth - The term “Future Jazz” didn’t exist in 1994 (neither as a genre nor as a catchphrase among DJs), but I wanted to give this new stylistic phenomenon a powerful (and provocative) name. Basically, it meant: this isn’t acid jazz (i.e. old stuff or old stuff played anew) but electronically produced music, mostly created by recluses in the studio, as opposed to live bands. To answer your question about whether I have a sense of pride: yes, at the very least I can claim that, with the FSOJ series, I helped found and shape this genre.JT - You have both been at the forefront of exploring and revealing the links between electronic music and jazz for decades. What has changed in your opinion? Michael Reinboth - Back then, as mentioned above, it was mostly individuals producing jazzy electronic music; today, there are far more collectives (perhaps the first being Jazzanova) that can also perform it live (the Cinematic Orchestra, for example). It always takes time (much longer for jazz than for techno) for the tracks to become more complex and sophisticated - that is, to delve deeper into the essence of jazz, discover something new, and master electronic equipment and production techniques at the same level. But there were phases when Future Jazz was flooded by Neo Disco, New Wave revivals, Trap, Lo-Fi, and Broken Techno. That was also one reason why the intervals between FSOJ events grew longer. At this point, I have to once again give a big shout-out to Michael Rütten, who really helped me get back on track with it.Michael Rütten - Many projects, bands and producers that combine both worlds (jazz and electronics) have appeared on the scene over the last 10-15 years. Probably a lot of them inspired by the likes of Jason Swinscoe‘s Cinematic Orchestra, Theo Parrish, Nicolas Jaar, Matthew Herbert, just to name a few. Contrast Trio out of Frankfurt is one of them, just re-united with a new approach, or Momoko Gill out of London, who combines classic songwriting and live played drums by herself with jazz, soul and electronic elements. Emanative aka Nick Woodmansey also produces and plays music with the live aspect in mind from scratch. DJ Oil from Marseille/Paris with his quite unique sound. So much has happened and is still happening on the forefront of music which sits somewhere in between genres. I think that the pandemic has also played a huge role regarding this point. Artists had to find a new way of expression and took the time to either re-invent themselves or/and explore new territories. Jazz is the teacher, always or let‘s say again. JT - There’s a deep and hypnotic aesthetic running throughout the compilation (with a few exceptions). This cosmic-ambient-krauty-repetition way of composition is something I’ve noticed myself a lot recently on labels like We Jazz, International Anthem and many others. Do you think that this is the natural result of a generation of jazz (and jazz-curious) musicians growing up knowing and understanding electronic music? Is it also a sign of the times? A human need to explore slowness and transcendence in an ever-crazier world?Michael Reinboth - Oh yes, I do think that slowing down and a certain catharsis - escaping this crazy world - is a reason to turn to this music more than ever. It helps; it heals a little.Michael Rütten - Well, that is something I’ve just realized while doing the tracklist for the CD/digital release of FSOJ 16! And yes, it‘s definitely a sign of the times we are living in. And also all things go round in circles. With the overload of overproduced music plus AI most recently, producers, musicians and people feel the need to slow down, dive into soul-soothing repetitive moments, going back to the roots actually. Be it via ancient rhythms, ambient (healing) sounds, it’s soulsearching in the end. Seeking warmth and something to hold on to in this mad world. Electronic music evolved out of repetitive elements, exploring of sounds and a very free approach, far from limiting forms of music theory. Bringing the human aspect more into the creation. It’s a very exciting time period right now! JT - It’s been four years since the last Future Jazz compilation which had quite a different feel to this new one - What do you see NOW that could be a new direction in another four years in the future?Michael Reinboth - It’s completely trend-independent, but Michael and I have a few older tracks with a disco vibe—disco jazz, so to speak. Let’s see if we can put together a ‘Future Sounds of Disco Jazz’ compilation with them. For Vol. 19 or 20, I could imagine something more hardcore tech-jazz.I’m curious to see how our Future Sounds of Jazz DJ gigs go. The sound has been totally underground for years and I hope that will change in four years. We’re working on it.  Michael Rütten - Like Michael Reinboth said: trend-independent is the word here. Timelessness, always forward thinking without following any trends. Just following our instinct, gut and feeling. BUY HERE! https://compostrecords.bandcamp.com/album/future-sounds-of-jazz-vol-16
items._cn_summary: 《Future Sounds of Jazz》第十六卷由慕尼黑独立厂牌Compost Records发行，创始人与长期电台主持人联合策划，延续了1995年开创的爵士与电子融合路线。专辑汇集了多位当代制作人和乐手的作品，横跨爵士感性的浩室、碎拍、电子实验与氛围化器乐演奏，强调自由律动与跨流派美学。厂牌长期致力于连接底特律高科技爵士传统与欧洲电子场景，本辑进一步拓展了音乐边界，曲目选择兼顾深度与多样性，是该系列三十一年来又一次高水准的汇编。整体制作思路强调音乐人之间的品味共鸣与策展对话，而非单一风格取向。

items.body: Breton producer Quinquis (Emilie Quinquis) has announced “scenes d’interieur”, her original soundtrack to Melanie Leray’s stage production of the same name. The five-track release comes out on 13 November 2026 via Mute. The multi-media production blends theatre and film as it follows Chloe, an actress preparing to perform the role of Nora in Henrik Ibsen’s “A Doll’s House.” The stage sections trace the breakdown of Chloe’s own relationship, while a parallel story shown on film covers her childhood, raised by a mother who survived domestic violence. Ibsen’s 1879 play, which caused a scandal on release for questioning the traditional roles of men and women in marriage, runs through both timelines, tying the production to themes of control and the search for emancipation. Quinquis’ score follows the two timelines, underscoring Chloe’s vulnerability, pain and strength as she navigates the violence of her stepfather as a teenager and of her husband as an adult in the present day. She uses modular electronics to score the live theatre performances and acoustic instrumentation for the film sections, extending the dialogue between past and present that runs through the production. The single “Lena” is an intimate piece where slow-moving synths give way to distant voices as the track builds through layers of emotion. The album was recorded on Ushant Island, off the coast of Brittany, where Quinquis lives, and features a track recorded with Amsterdam-based labelmate Desire Marea, “Inkanuko.” “scenes d’interieur” (catalogue number iMUTE703) carries five tracks: “Chloe,” “Nora,” “Puzuilhan,” “Inkanuko” and “Lena.” It follows Quinquis’ 2025 album “eor” and the 2024 single “Morwreg”, both also released via Mute. About Quinquis Quinquis is the project of Breton producer Emilie Quinquis, based on Ushant Island off the coast of Brittany. Her work moves between electronic and acoustic instrumentation, built around modular synthesis, field recording and a close relationship to the Breton coast where she lives. Quinquis released the “aer” EP and the album “SEIM” before “Morwreg” preceded her 2025 album “eor,” both issued via Mute. “scenes d’interieur,” her soundtrack to Melanie Leray’s stage production of the same name, follows in November 2026 and marks her first release built specifically for a theatre production, combining her modular electronic work for the live stage sections with acoustic instrumentation for the production’s film sequences.

items._cn_summary: 布列塔尼制作人Quinquis为Melanie Leray的舞台剧创作了原创配乐，作品融合剧场与影像两条时间线。舞台段落以模块化电子合成器处理，影片段落使用原声乐器配乐，两者在过去与现在的对话中互相延伸。专辑在布列塔尼海岸的乌尚岛录制，创作围绕一位演员准备出演易卜生《玩偶之家》中娜拉的过程展开，将剧中对婚姻角色与挣脱束缚的追问映射到角色的个人创伤上。单曲《Lena》以缓慢移动的合成器逐步叠加远处人声，层层累积情绪张力。另收录与厂牌同门Desire Marea合作的《Inkanuko》。整体声音设计兼顾亲密感与戏剧张力，将电子实验、原声写作与剧场叙事结合为统一的听觉体验。

items.body: 〈過剰〉を〈過剰〉のままで―沖澤のどか／SKOの《トゥランガリーラ交響曲》｜内野 儀 Excess in All Its Excess: Nodoka Okisawa and the SKO’s Turangalîla-Symphonie 2026年8月23日 キッセイ文化ホール（長野県松本文化会館） セイジ・オザワ 松本フェスティバル オーケストラ コンサート Aプログラム（2日目） 2026/8/23 Kissei Culture Hall (Nagano Prefecture Matsumoto Culture Hall) 2026 Seiji Ozawa Matsumoto Festival: Orchestral Concert — Program A (Day 2) Reviewed by 内野 儀(UCHINO, Tadashi) Photos by 山田毅(Takeshi Yamada)／2026OMF :大窪道治 （Michiharu Okubo）／2026OMF 〈演奏〉 指揮：沖澤のどか ピアノ：務川慧悟 オンド・マルトノ：原田節 管弦楽：サイトウ・キネン・オーケストラ 〈曲目〉 オリヴィエ・メシアン《トゥランガリーラ交響曲》 ©山田毅／2026OMF 《トゥランガリーラ交響曲》は、あらゆる意味で〈過剰〉な作品である。85分、10楽章、100人を超える大編成オーケストラ。独奏ピアノとオンド・マルトノ、数多くの打楽器奏者、そしてピアノ・チェレスタ・鍵盤グロッケンシュピール・ヴィブラフォンからなる「ガムラン」群。ティンパニもハープもない代わりに、これだけのものが投入されている。 〈過剰〉は規模にとどまらない。メシアン自身、第1楽章の中間部を「ポリリズム、ポリモダリティ、ポリミュージック」と呼んだ(1)第4楽章の再現部については、スケルツォ主題、ピアノ独奏、コントラバスのピツィカート、ガムラン群、リズム・ペダルを奏するウッドブロック、小トルコ・シンバル、小太鼓のリズム、木管とホルンの第1トリオ、弦の第2トリオ、そしてトロンボーンの第一循環主題（〈彫像の主題〉）——10の独立した音楽が同時に鳴ると自ら数え上げている（Messiaen, p. 227; Shenton, p. 49）。したがって、打楽器奏者には「第六感」をもちあわせた第一級の精度が必要で、小さな誤りひとつで音楽が壊れる、と書き残している（p.156; p.15）。 メシアンはまた、「歓びの讃歌(hymn to joy)」と本作を形容するが、その「歓び」の定義そのものが〈過剰〉である。「17世紀の実直なブルジョワ市民が味わうような穏やかで満ち足りた歓びではない」と否定形からその定義を始め、「不幸のただなかにあってかろうじて垣間見た者だけが思い描きうるもの、超人的で、溢れ出し、目を眩ませ、過剰なものだ」と書く（p.151; p.6）。「愛」についても、「トリスタンとイゾルデの媚薬によって象徴されるような、すべてを超え、自らの外にあるすべてを消し去る宿命的で抗いがたい愛」であるとする（同上）。この「愛」が、媚薬による絶対的／超越的「愛」である以上、そこに暴力性が畳み込まれているのは当然である。実際、冒頭でトロンボーンが重い3度で叩きつける第一循環主題を、メシアンは〈彫像の主題〉と呼び、メキシコの記念建造物の恐るべき残酷さを喚起するものと説明している(2)。要するに、この作品において〈過剰〉は方法や結果ではない。〈過剰〉こそが主題である。 そのことを考えるとき、私はどうしても作曲年代のことを思う。1945年6月25日、セルゲイ・クーセヴィツキーがメシアンに委嘱状を書いた。ドイツ降伏の7週間後である。メシアンの返信は8月20日、《ハラウィ(Harawi)》を書き上げつつあったプティシェ(Petichet)のサマーホームからで、「美しく、相応の規模をもった作品を書きたい。そのためには夢み、愛し、練り上げ、急がずに管弦楽化する時間が要る」だった(3)。 ソプラノとピアノのための連作歌曲《ハラウィ》(1945）、この《トゥランガリーラ交響曲》（1946–48）、無伴奏12声のための《5つのルシャン》（1948）。のちにトリスタン三部作と呼ばれる三作は、この数年のうちに続けて書かれた。編成も規模もまったく異なるが、いずれも愛と死をめぐる同じ主題系のもとにある。メシアンの作品のなかで、カトリック信仰を直接の主題としない数少ない例でもある。 同じ1945年の秋、メシアンにはもうひとつ差し迫った委嘱があった。アンリ・バロー(Henry Barraud)からの、戦時中の強制移送者を追悼する作品である。11月2日の演奏会に向けて、9月22日——《ハラウィ)》完成の1週間後——に楽譜を渡せるように《強制移送者たちの歌（Chant des déportés）》を書き、さらに、10月10日の日記には、「クーセヴィツキーのために交響的作品を書く」と記している(4)。 戦時中の強制移送者を追悼する作品と、この巨大な交響曲の初期的構想とは、同じ数週間のなかにあった。作曲そのものは1946年7月17日から1948年11月29日まで(p.151; p.4)行われたが、作曲者自身についても、よく知られているように、自らが収監されていたゲルリッツの捕虜収容所で《世の終わりのための四重奏曲》を1941年に書いて演奏もしている(5)。 1945年5月16日——ドイツ降伏の8日後——にメシアンが雑誌『ヴォロンテ(Volontés)』へ寄せた文章がある。「現代音楽には乾いた非人間的なものが多すぎる！」とかれは書く。「来たるべき革新者は言語だけの革命家であってはならない。絶望の塊や、人の住まない惑星ではなく、大文字の愛を」。そして、待ち望まれている「解放者」、すなわち「愛の作曲家」の到来をともに祈ってくれと呼びかけている(6)。「絶望の塊」。「人の住まない惑星」。「解放者」。1945年5月のヨーロッパで書かれた語彙である。 この交響曲が戦争を描いていると言いたいのではない。標題にも、作曲者の膨大な自己解説のどこにも、そんなことは書かれていない。だが、これほどの規模の肯定が何に対する応答だったのかを問わずに済ませることもできないのではないか。「不幸のただなかで垣間見た者だけが思い描きうる歓び」——この条件節に、1946年のヨーロッパで指示対象がなかったとは、私には考えにくい。廃墟の記憶は、フランスが戦勝国であったからといって消えるようなものではない。 専門家ではないので見落としが多いことだろうが、短期間ではあるものの目を通すことができた英語文献にかぎると、メシアンと戦争をめぐる議論は《四重奏曲》と占領期に集中しているようで、トリスタン三部作のほうは、もっぱら二つの方向に読まれてきた印象が残る。ひとつは本作についてのシュルレアリスム的プログラムの解読、もうひとつは作曲者の私生活——病んでゆく最初の妻クレール・デルボスと、イヴォンヌ・ロリオとの関係——への還元である。 後者は、私にはあまり実りがあるとは思えない。第一に、メシアン自身が私生活と作品を明示的に結びつけていない。シェントンも、まさにその理由でその論点を扱わないと断っている(7)。第二に、そもそも個人的な恋愛の高揚だけでは、この規模と構造を説明しきれない。この規模は、私的な感情の器としては明らかに大きすぎる。 もちろん、〈過剰〉は、説明されるべき欠陥ではない。これは端的に誇大妄想である。あるいは、過大妄想とでもいうべきか。初演前のNBCの放送でクーセヴィツキーは、《春の祭典》に次ぐ今世紀最大の作品だと言い切った(8)。誇大／過大な言い方である。だが誇大／過大であることこそが、この作品の内容なのだと思う。廃墟のあとに、この規模で〈愛〉と〈歓び〉を主張すること。〈まっとう〉な振る舞いではない。そして、〈まっとう〉ではないことが必要だったのではないか。 メシアンは1953年、自分は神秘主義の音楽家ではなくシュルレアリストの音楽家である、ただしその超現実への欲望は超自然によって超えられている、と述べている(9)。シェントンはこの発言を、ブルトンの『シュルレアリスム第二宣言』（1930）に重ねている。ブルトンがそこで求めたのは、「生と死、現実と想像、過去と未来、伝達可能性と伝達不可能性、高と低がもはや矛盾として知覚されなくなるような精神の一点」(10)であった。第一次大戦後に成立したシュルレアリスムの論理が、戦後期のメシアンの自己規定に重ねられる。歓びと恐怖を対立させないこと、〈愛の主題〉と〈彫像の主題〉とを同じ作品に置くこと。それは意匠ではなく、あの時代への応答となる思想として、私には聴こえる。 だから、この作品を単一の陶酔へ向かって収束させる聴き方には、私は与しない。緩徐楽章の〈愛の主題〉に匂い立つような官能を求め、終曲に忘我を求める——そうした期待は、作品の多層性を単一の陶酔へ狭める読みだと思う。 サンスクリットの題、ヒンドゥーのターラ、ガムラン、メキシコの記念建造物、ボスとシャガールとピラネージ。快楽の園と出口のない牢獄。この作品が抱え込んでいるものは、どこまでも多元的であり、その多元性には〈地獄的なもの〉まで含まれている。二元論を拒むこと、一つの中心へ回収されないこと。それが、この〈過剰〉の設計思想である。 ©大窪道治／2026OMF 23日の演奏は、まさにそれを鳴らした。沖澤のどかはこの日、指揮棒を持たずに振った。打点を棒で叩き込まない身ぶりが奏者に過剰な圧をかけず、テンポは「押される」のではなく「走り出す」。第5楽章や終曲の疾走感は、絶対的なテンポの速さからではなく、その場その場の奏者との呼吸から生まれてくる。〈自然体〉、という言い方がふさわしい。 そしてこの〈自然体〉は、〈過剰〉を手なずけるための方便ではなかった。同時多発は同時多発のまま残り、しかしカオスにはならない。第2楽章冒頭で三つの群が別々のリズムを刻む箇所も、ガムラン群が主要主題と併走する箇所も、均されることなく、それぞれの層として聴こえてくる。沖澤は公演前に、「すべてをクリアにすることによって濃厚にしたい」と語っていた。「どこまでも緻密に作ったうえで、それを体に沁み込ませる。そして、オーケストラが曲を知り尽くした状態にしたうえで本番に自由になるような——そこを目指」す、とも(11)。明晰さは削減ではない。〈過剰〉が混濁ではなく〈過剰〉として聴こえるための、重要な条件の一つである。抑制でも整理でもなく、〈過剰〉を〈過剰〉のまま、リアルタイムに立ち上げること。この作品にこれほど相応しい方法があるだろうか。 その姿勢が最も明瞭に出たのが、第8楽章の終わりである。「愛の展開」と題されたこの楽章では、〈和音の主題〉がよく聞こえる。だがこの楽章は〈彫像の主題〉で閉じられる。しかもその最後の音は、管楽器から、タムタム、大太鼓、ピアノ、コントラバスへと受け渡される。打たれた瞬間から消えはじめる音である。「愛の展開」が行き着いた先に、この落下がある。減衰を聴きつづけるあいだ、それが恐ろしいのか美しいのかは判別できない。沖澤はその減衰を、かなりの長さにわたって聴かせた。急ぐ理由がないから急がない。それだけのことが、この作品ではほとんど過激に響く。他方、全曲を締める終曲の最後は、極端に引き延ばされることなく、比較的速いポイントですっきりと切り上げられた。 四つの循環主題のうち、メシアンが唯一象徴的意味を与えなかったのが〈和音の主題〉である。かれはこれを、主題というよりも異なる音の層を成り立たせるための口実だと言い、中世錬金術の標語を引いている——分離し、そして凝固させよ。要素へと分解し、新たな形へ組み直す(12)。この日の演奏が全曲にわたっておこなっていたのは、まさにその作業だった。 ©山田毅／2026OMF 務川慧悟のピアノは、第1楽章のカデンツァから第5楽章の強打まで、和音の一音一音が分離して聴こえる明晰さを保った。強奏でも音が濁らない。舞台前方下手側にピアノ、チェレスタ、鍵盤グロッケンシュピール、ヴィブラフォン、上手側にオンド・マルトノという配置で、鍵盤・打楽器群の合奏はきわめて緊密だった。原田節のオンド・マルトノは、前から13列目やや下手寄りという私の席では音量的に前に出てこず、弦との溶け合いのなかに沈む場面が多かった。席位置による部分が大きいだろう。 緩急の振幅も、極大から極小まで振り切ったダイナミクスの幅も、「楽譜どおり」と言ってしまえばそれまでかもしれない。だが今回聴こえたのは、楽譜の指示の「再現」ではなく「現実化」だった。書かれていることが、その場で実際に起きるのだ。 私には、廃墟の記憶のうえに立つ〈まっとう〉ではない規模の肯定として聴こえた。それは一つの答えに収束することを拒み、多元的なまま、〈過剰〉なまま鳴りつづけるように感じられた。きな臭さを増していく2026年の日本で、その〈過剰〉が整理も馴致もされずに響いたことには、意味があると思う。純粋な音楽として、である。 （2026/9/15) 註 (1)Messiaen, O. (1995). Traité de rythme, de couleur, et d’ornithologie. Volume 2, Paris: Alphonse Leduc, p.163. Shenton, Andrew. Olivier Messiaen’s Turangalîla-symphonie (Elements in Music since 1945) , London: Cambridge UP, 2023, p.41からの孫引き。上掲書からの引用はシェントンの著作による。和訳はシェントン本の英語からの拙訳。以下、同書からの引用については、両書の頁数のみを記す。 (2) Quoted in Shenton, p.36. (3)ナイジェル・シメオン(Nigel Simeone)によるハイペリオンCDA67816ライナーノート(2012)の記述による。https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W14114_67816。シェントンもまた、シメオンの記述を引用している（p.4）。 (4)Ibid. (5)《世の終わりのための四重奏曲》についての、メシアンが収監されていた捕虜収容所での演奏や解放後の同曲の経緯については、Leslie A. Sprout, “Messiaen, Jolivet, and the Soldier–Composers of Wartime France”, The Musical Quarterly 87, no. 2 (2004): pp. 259–304に詳しい。 (6) Quoted in Shenton, p.21. (7)Shenton, p.35. (8)Quoted in Shenton, p.1. エピグラフとして引用されているが、1949年11月28日、NBCにおけるオリン・ダウンズ（Olin Downes）との対話である。 (9)Quoted in Shenton, p.18. (10)Shenton, p.18. (11)「 J-WAVE NEWS」2026年7月28日(https://news.j-wave.co.jp/2026/07/content-5509.html)。 (12) Shenton, p.38.シェントンが本書で引用するメシアン自身による循環主題についての説明は、1991年のドイツグラモフォン版の録音に付されたライナーノートによる。 [Performers] Conductor: Nodoka Okisawa Piano: Keigo Mukawa Ondes Martenot: Takashi Harada Orchestra: Saito Kinen Orchestra [Program] Olivier Messiaen: Turangalîla-Symphonie
items._cn_summary: 本乐评聚焦于冲澤のどか指挥サイトウ・キネン・オーケストラ演绎梅西安《图伦加利拉交响曲》的现场演出。乐评以〈過剰〉为核心线索，从作品分析延伸至历史语境：指出作品在时长、编制、节奏与和声上均体现极度的复杂性与规模，同时引用梅西安本人对「欢悦」与「爱」的定义——超越性、淹没性、近乎暴力的强度。乐评特别将创作置于1945年战后欧洲的历史背景中，串联《被强制迁徙者之歌》《图伦加利拉》《五首雷尚》等作品的连续写作脉络，质疑战后废墟记忆如何渗入这部表面欢悦的巨作。评论还触及学界对此作品解读的两条路径——超现实主义程式与作曲家私生活，并暗示需要更严肃地审视其历史语境。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are classic bands whose lineups become fixed in time, beyond any later variations, as the very ones through which we first discovered them; these are the lineups that produced a handful of classic albums, creating the impression (or illusion) that they could do no wrong. This happened with the Peter Gabriel-era Genesis in the 70s, with Yes during the time Bruford and Wakeman were in the band, and in many other cases, given that the decade was so rich and vast it seemed endless, and it happened with Roxy Music. However, what set Roxy Music apart was that, alongside Bryan Ferry, possessing a voice that was glamorous yet capable of sounding menacing when needed, and Andy Mackay (on sax and oboe, coaxing out an incredible sonic range), and Phil Manzanera (a guitarist who possessed undeniable credentials in an era when every self-respecting guitarist had to prove their worth), and Paul Thompson (on drums, anchoring a sextet with such great chemistry), there was Brian Eno. He was the element that would disrupt any sense of equilibrium, or, conversely, help them find balance within the very imbalance that made them unique."Re-Make / Re-Model" kicks off without asking for permission; Manzanera's guitar seems to attack, and the same goes for Ferry's vocals, almost punk before punk existed. They sounded frenetic, with McKay's sax channeling free jazz, and were expertly backed by Graham Simpson's bass. Brian Eno's signature backing vocals and synthesizer interventions were already present; he brought the electronics, he brought modernity. You can sense the freedom and the way they play around with interruptions (including a nod to the Beatles) during the pauses before the finale. Ferry was not just a singer with a distinct personality; he also contributed significantly on the piano with his dissonant notes. They had fun experimenting in the studio, and that spirit was captured on the record; the proof is that it sounds like a live album."Ladytron" opens with a space-rock feel; Mackay's oboe displays a subtlety echoed by Ferry, revealing a facet of the band completely different from the previous track. The sound then seems to shift toward the Canterbury scene, with the saxophone and guitar sharing the lead, at times epic, at others drifting aimlessly without vying for the spotlight. "If There Is Something" surprises with a country-western atmosphere, yet the band transforms it into glam rock in the vein of Bowie or Elton John; then, Manzanera's Black Sabbath-esque solo tears us away from the Wild West, while Ferry sings as only he could, at times reminiscent of Family's Roger Chapman."Virginia Plain" would become one of the band's classics from this early period, featuring the humor in Ferry's vocals combined with Eno's synthesizer work, all within a track that remained, at its core, rock 'n' roll in their own distinctive style: an avant-garde approach devoid of solemnity, which is precisely why we still love it so much.The wonderful thing about this debut was its variety; as we shifted to something more serious and experimental with "2HB," Ferry's voice transported us to space epics and evoked a yearning for a bohemian past, something he harbored even in his youth at the time, which also gave the band a modern edge. Paul Thompson varied the rhythms, introducing more syncopation, while the saxophone's intensity receded, leaving Eno's keyboards to persist, looping over and over, and making us feel as though we were inside Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.We are talking about space, and it feels as though we are plunging into a black hole of unknown destination; "The Bob (Medley)" kicks off, following the intro, with an epic rock sound driven by saxophones reminiscent of Van der Graaf Generator and Ferry's defiant vocals. Then comes a medieval section, echoes of the past, fitting for a band as cinematic as Roxy Music (especially during this era) followed by raw, wild rock, yet punctuated by synthesizers that feel like blocks of ice in the desert, alongside Mackay's frenetic oboe. And when Ferry's piano notes arrive, and the guitar soars like thunder in a storm, making its presence powerfully felt, we know this band is like no other."Chance Meeting" is one of those very special tracks that seem not to have been composed on Earth, possessing a strange beauty and a strange melody; it certainly resembles contemporary classical music, dissonant and asymmetrical, with an architecture that defies established conventions. This is because the piano and Ferry's calm, simmering vocals contrast with Manzanera's guitar, which cuts through the air like a power saw.If you think Would You Believe settles into calm and normalcy, you are mistaken; Ferry's obsession with nostalgia takes us, for the first time, though not the last, back to the 50s, but in a wild, street-level style."Sea Breezes" once again pushes the boundaries of the avant-garde with an Eastern-tinged melody where Ferry's voice takes center stage, shining like the marquee lights of an old theater in a seaside town where seagulls bear eternal witness to the people passing through year after year. The music conjures images and stirs emotions; it seems to repeat itself yet introduces subtle shifts, unfolding slowly, like the passing years, almost imperceptibly. Beneath the layers of wildness and impetuosity lay wisdom and deliberate structure; Paul Thompson knew exactly when to make his entrance, and just as the oboe plays a delicate melody, Manzanera cuts through it with his guitar, creating a harmony born of chaos. When Ferry sings, it is as if he is backed by a strange orchestra, strange, indeed, but an orchestra nonetheless.Precisely by downplaying an era that seemed to be growing increasingly serious, they conclude with a simple, almost a cappella melody titled "Bitter's End", a tune reminiscent of an old village, quintessentially English, fully aware that every avant-garde movement follows its own unique path.

items._cn_summary: 这张1972年的首张专辑将华丽摇滚、前卫实验与自由爵士元素融为一体，呈现出别具一格的英式艺术摇滚风貌。Brian Ferry的钢琴与嗓音兼具魅力与威胁感，Andy Mackay的萨克斯与双簧管拓展了宽广的音色空间，Phil Manzanera的吉他既有自由爵士的狂躁也有黑色安息日式的厚重段落，Brian Eno的合成器介入则为整体注入了现代电子色彩与不稳定的平衡感。专辑在曲目编排上展现高度实验性，从开场曲的准朋克冲力到太空摇滚、坎特伯雷即兴、乡村西部元素的并置，结构自由且充满玩心。整张唱片捕捉到乐手在录音室中即兴碰撞的化学反应，听感如同现场录音般鲜活，在当时开创了一种既前卫又不失俏皮的摇滚美学。

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Undoubtedly one of the great surprises of this year is the release of King Gizzard's full-blown EDModyssey 'Alien Metal', which is their twenty-eight studio album to date. The follow-up to 2025's'Phantom Island' sees the Australian band abandoning all rock instrumentation for a futuristic beat-driven, techno-inspired rave sound, utilizing a modular synth system that allows them to explore avast range of sequenced rhythms, electronic textures, and an overall synthetic, club-orientedproduction style. Contemporary bands rarely do such dramatic stylistic shifts, but this acid-ladencreation from the kings of psychedelic blues turns out to be a fun and engaging listen (that willnevertheless shock many dedicated fans), that is above all else, a finely constructed electronicwork, wherein each tracks flows into the next one, giving the impression of a massive piece ofprogressive house. Within this mixture of quirky techno beats, bassy breakbeats, and ambientinterludes, the ominous alien-like robotic vocals that wiggle their way through, give 'Alien Metal'somewhat of a sci-fi edge. However, despite all of the pristine synth sequences and polished studiosound, the occasional repetitiveness of this album can potentially lead to listener fatigue.Moreover, the synthetic club feel provides for a great background listen, but is there really thatmuch substance to dig into upon repeated listens? The tracks that I enjoy the most on 'Alien Metal'are the punchy opener 'Sapience', which beautifully transitions into the excellent title track,followed by the powerful and mesmerizing 'Level 5', and the trippy 'Uqt', which appears towards theend. The album finale is strong, too, while the entire work feels intentionally futuristic andvibrant, which is perhaps what most listeners would cling to.
items._genre: electronic / techno / acid / progressive house / psychedelic
items._cn_summary: 澳大利亚乐队King Gizzard的第二十八张录音室专辑彻底放弃了所有摇滚乐器，转向纯粹电子化制作。整张作品依托模块化合成器系统构建，融合科技舞曲节奏、碎拍与氛围间奏，呈现出俱乐部取向的酸性电子声响。机器人化的人声处理增添了科幻色彩，曲目之间无缝衔接，形成统一的渐进浩室整体感。开篇曲与同名曲衔接流畅，中段的层次递进以及末尾的迷幻段落尤为突出。评论者肯定其在风格急转弯后依然保持了结构上的连贯与趣味，但同时指出部分段落存在重复感，深层可挖掘的内容有限，更偏向氛围化的背景聆听体验。整体而言，这是一次从迷幻摇滚向电子领域的大胆跨越，制作精良但实验深度仍有提升空间。
