items.body: （14）遠方より無へ（Ⅲ）『ノエシス』の「異常な空想」 Text by 丘山万里子（Mariko Okayama） 『ノエシス』（1978）について、『レオス』の改作を、との気持ちで長期間それを眺めていたものの、放棄したことは先述した。「かなり深みにはまった」その迷いとは、長く親しんだフランス実存主義と、未だ茫漠たる無空世界の間にあって、自分をどこに置くか、の問い。『王孫不帰』（1970）から『レクイエム』を挟んでのこの時期、彼のなかにずっとあった「ある一つの情感」、すなわち死者（母も含む）への情念（パトス）の切迫を、いかに音で「葬う」ことができようか、だったろう。 平たく言えば、「情」（パトス）に竿さす危うさからいったん身を引き「理知」（ロゴス）へと足を移す必要があったということで、このあたりのバランス感覚はいかにも三善らしい（パトス、ロゴスといった語彙は三善が使用）。サルトルの『存在と無』経由でフッサールの意識の現象学へ遡行した彼の目論見は、作品タイトルとなった「ノエシス」（意識作用）の音楽化（響きと持続）だ。 まずは、三善の自作解説を見よう。 「新作は定量記譜により、いくつかの楽器群が固有の持続をもちながら相互参加する関係を統合した。フルートとオーボエの、クラリネットの、金管の、弦の、それぞれの群、その他クローシュなど、個々の楽器の“音楽”は、音が（その空白を含めてアプリオリに）時間をもっている、という意味で私の存在感覚に属するが、志向性をもたない。フッサール流にこれをヒューレ（ママ）とするならば、それらが一個全体の持続のために（志向的に）存在しはじめるには、そのための契機あるいは生気を与えるノエシスが、やはり私の体験裡に、しかし対自的な意識作用として、つまり、異常な空想の体験として、なければならない。“迷い”と前述したが、それもかなり深みにはまったこの期間に、自己離脱的にこのノエシスが強められていったかと思われる。それは、いつも、そうしていたことなのかもしれないが。」（『遠方より無へ』p.161） そもそも「ノエシス」という哲学用語も一般人には意味不明、解説も難解。この文章の前には、改作に「次第に心咎められ」、「全ての音が、それぞれのありようでそこにあり、そこから生まれる投企は別のところにある。その投企を追うことは、別の創作でしかない。迷いだった。」との記述がある。哲学的厳密考察はおき（私には無理）、荒っぽく眺めると、「投企」「対自的」「自己離脱」はサルトル、「志向性」「ヒュレー」「ノエシス」「意識作用」はフッサールといった具合に哲学用語が散りばめられており、三善の頭の中にこれらが「異常な空想」として飛び交っていたことが知れる。 それは、どんな音楽になったか？ たまたまこの8月（2026/8/8 尾高忠明指揮、東京都交響楽団＠東京芸術劇場）に『ノエシス』実演があった。私は実演に接したことはなく、手元の書籍・楽譜・音源（初演録音1978/尾高指揮・東フィルなど）でこういう作品、的理解をしていたが、大きな衝撃を受けた。作品は音が楽譜に定着された時点で、自立した命をそこに宿す。尾高と都響が描き出す『ノエシス』の明晰かつ凛烈なドラマトゥルギーは三善の何たるか（というのもおかしいのだが）を確然と示し、意識作用云々の理屈など押し退け冴えざえと美しく、しかも、やはり『レオス』の流れを汲むもの、と聴こえたのだ。端的に言えば、冒頭と終尾に響くチェロ独奏が宿す世界がそれ。同時に「反戦三部作」のやはり都響一挙実演で（本稿第1回）、ふと浮かび上がる歌の欠片に三善の「声」を聴いた（同じ首席チェロ奏者）、そのことを思い出させた。 が、それはいったん傍に置き、本作におけるフッサール援用の要点を拾いつつ、三善の「異常な空想」模様を眺めてみたい。 以下、あくまで三善の『ノエシス』（作品と自作解説）を背景にしつつのフッサール理解とする。 【『ノエシス』とフッサール現象学】―ノエシス・ノエマ・ヒュレー この世界にひしめく「事物（モノ）現象（コト）：事象」に対するにあたり、その「本質」を認知識別する人間の「意識」に分け入り、その事象の成り立つところを厳密な「学」として記述したのがフッサールの「現象学」（「事象そのものへ」（Zu den Sachen selbst））。フッサールはこれを「ノエシス （Noesis）」（意識作用）、「ノエマ（Noema）」（対象：事象）、「ヒュレー（Hyle） 」（素材）の3要素から解く。 「ヒュレー」とは人間の感覚器官（五感：視、聴、触、味、嗅）による感受で、それ自体は何ら意味を持たない「感覚的体験」（『イデーンⅠ−Ⅱ』p.91~93）。この諸体験を「生気づける“意味付与的な”（もしくは意味付与を本質的に内含するところの）一つの層」がそこには横たわっており、この層からノエマに向かう「志向性」（「意識は常に何ものかへ向かう」）が生じる。この志向性に基づき、バラバラな感覚的諸体験に何らかの意味を与え、統合・統一をはかるのが「ノエシス」（意識作用）で、この働きによって「ノエマ」(対象) が現出する、という図柄だ。 三善はこのヒュレーを、個々の楽器の持つ固有性（持続：時間を含む）とみなす。が、彼にとってフルート、オーボエ、クラリネット、クローシュなどなどの楽器は単なるヒュレー（素材）ではなく、「個々の楽器の“音楽”は、音が時間をもっている（その空白も含めてアプリオリに）という意味で自分の“存在感覚”に属する」。ここで存在感覚、とは三善の音への生理とでも言えようか。音に「輪郭」が見え、「イメージ」があり、「ポエジー」を感じる彼にとって、「楽器音」はすでにある種の志向性を含む。フッサールも感覚的体験がすでに意味を内包する場合もあるとしており（ex.上述引用「本質的に内含」）、私はこれを潜在的志向性（アプリオリ）を持つヒュレーと考える。この、潜在的志向性を持つヒュレー（楽器音）は、けれども、個から全体へ関連付け、統合する明確な一つの志向性は、持たない。個々の楽器の「音楽」（「音」ではない）が「一個全体の持続のために（志向的に）存在し始めるためには、そのための契機あるいは生気を与えるノエシスが、やはり私の体験裡に、しかし対自的な意識作用として、つまり、異常な空想の体験として、なければならない。」 つまりヒュレー（楽器音）が内包する潜在的志向性に基づき、一つの全体としての統合・総合体へと連関させるノエシスの作用は、自分の場合、どのような音楽表現としてノエマへと至りうるのか（象を結び得るか）、ということだ。 現象学は神の視点から人間の視点へと西欧精神世界が移行した時期の思潮・哲学の一つだが、その援用は、神にも仏にも依拠しない「根こそぎ喪失者」である三善が、今一度、人間の意識そのものを「凝視すべく」（眺めるのでなく）対自的に課した「自分の裡なる西欧（実存主義）」についての自己点検作業だったと言えよう（「自己離脱的にこのノエシスが強められていった」）。 【相関性と本質直感】 だが、上記3要素を下図とする意識の「作用」あるいは「働き」への着目は同時に、フッサール言うところの「相関性」（相互作用）や「本質直感」が何であるかをも、三善に示唆したに違いない。「ノエマ（相関項）と本質を混同してはならない。」（『イデーンⅢ』p.109）、「意識は精密に規定されえない流動する本質を有している。」（『イデーンⅡ―Ⅱ』p.151）、「本質感取は、原的に与える働きをする直感なのであり、本質をその“生身のありありとした”自己性において把握するものとなっているのである。」（『イデーンⅠ―Ⅰ』p.66）といった「本質」の絶対定立の否定、相互連関性（関係の網目）、流動性（変化する動態）、あるいは「生身のありありとした」（あるがままの）地平のイメージと「直感力」は、当時の三善の中の東洋的思惟とそのまま繋がるものであったろう。 フッサール現象学の持つこうした側面は、サルトル、メルロ＝ポンティ、エマニュエル・レヴィナス、ジャック・デリダらを通し様々に展開されてゆくが、三善が1988年12人の対談者と行った対談集には彼らの名前・語彙がしばしば登場している（『現代の芸術視座を求めて 対話十二章〜三善晃対談集』1989）。また、ノエシス、ノエマ、ヒュレーが具体的に語られるシーンもあり、彼がどんなイメージをそこに抱いていたかが読み取れる。 その中の一つ、多田美波（彫刻家）との対話を挙げておく（『現代の芸術視座を求めて』p.126~127）。 三善：素材が精製される過程では素材自身のルールに従うけれども、多田さんはそれを方向づけるのですから、素材にとって多田さんは契機となる。作品ができると、自然と作品とが契機を取り交わし合う。それを見る人は、その人の人生と天象の中での作品との出会いが契機になる。触発といってもいいけれども、当事者の転機のきっかけという意味で、契機でしょうね。ノエマとノエシスがずっとつながっていく。 素材はヒュレー。この素材について、多田は素材にも物にも人格のようなものがあり、「何か丸めて作って、自分の手の中でそれをつぶしてしまうことは非常に怖い。だから常にものを作りながらあっちへ置いておいて、途中でもこれに惚れ込むとか入り込むとかせず、常に対話しながら作っていかないと作品自体の性格、物の形ができてゆかない。」（要約）と述べており、これは前述のヒュレーに内在する潜在的志向性と言えよう。三善の「楽器音」と同じ存在感覚だ。かつ、全てが契機として働くその相互作用（対話）によって「志向性」（意味の付与・形）がおのずから発現し、その都度、ノエシス（働き）はノエマを形づくるが、そのノエシスとノエマもまたダイナミックな相関の連鎖として「ずっとつながってゆく」流動体、という螺旋の輪（輪廻とも言える）がここに見えてこよう。 このイメージこそ、本作に先立つ『シェーヌ』（1973）の鎖に他なるまい。ヒュレー・ノエシス・ノエマの3要素のいずれもが単体として分節されず、互いに撚り綯われつつ「流動する本質」の生成へと働き続けるさま。おそらく三善がフッサールから摘み取った「空想」（別に「異常」ではなかろう）は、これだ。フッサールは、想像力こそ「本質直感」だ、と言ってもいるし。 なお、多田は素材と自分との間の関係を「対話」と表現しているが、対談集での12人との対話はそれぞれの創造の場で創作家がいかにこれらの「関係」を意識しているかが自分の言葉で語られており、それを自己流に翻訳（解釈）する三善の「意識」が炙り出され非常に奥深いものとなっている。1988年の12ヶ月毎月1人ずつと対談したこの記録には、他者との会話の中に、三善がパリ留学からここまで歩いた道のりを振り返り、言語化し、自己確認する姿がはっきり見える。前回触れた井筒俊彦の「存在の絶対無分節的真相」の深淵、すなわち「深層意識」はフッサールの本質直感に重なろうし、三善はこの直感をさまざまに対談者と確認、いわば東西の「存在の地平」を模索している。 当時の『音楽芸術』編集者の用意したこの小さな船旅の前書き（ではないとの断りがあるが）末尾には、「対談という“楽譜”から、“ほんとの音”が立ち現れる予感…フッサールはこの快い緊張を名付けているだろうか」とある。 『ノエシス』とは、そういう位置にあるのだ。 この対談集については、後日、改めて触れよう。 にしても、どの時代であれ、その時代時代を先導する哲人とは、誰にとっても必要なことごとを、本人にとってのギリギリまで突き詰め書き尽くし、それを手にするそれぞれが、そこから自分に必要なターム、原理を引き出すことができるよう、そこここに無意識（深層意識）にこの本質直感の嘆息を「漏らしている」ように思う。全ての名作・名品がそうであるように。楽譜もむろん同じで、ゆえこそ実演がその都度それを開示し続けてゆくのだ。 【現象学と十二支縁起】 ことのついでに、このフッサールの現象学は第12回で紹介した仏教の理法、「十二支縁起」とほぼ重なることを指摘しておく。再度その縁起を引用するが、先に両者照合を大雑把にまとめると以下。 ノエマ：対象 ノエシス：心作用（行・識・名色） ヒュレー：六処（五感でなく六感で、第六感は五感を超える本質直感） 志向性：触・受・愛（愛は執着で、理を超えた最大の志向性と言えよう） かつ、これら十二要素が因果の連鎖であるとの認識（十二支縁起）は、フッサールの相互連関と本質流動、そのもの。 三善の「ノエマとノエシスがずっとつながっていく」とのイメージの仏教版と思ってよかろう。 つまり、フッサールもブッダも同じところを見ており、言語こそ違え、「要素：支（枝の意）」「相互連関：縁起（因果）」についての認識は等しい。これが、根源的原理抽出の普遍、あるいは人類普遍の「叡智」ということではないか。三善がそれを直覚していた、と前回述べたのもそれだ。 根本的な愚かさ（無明）によって対象に向かう心作用（行）があり、対象に向かう心作用によって判断作用（識）があり、判断作用によってその対象としての名称とかたちあるもの（名色）があり、名称とかたちあるものによって六つの感覚器官（六処）があり、六つの感覚器官によって対象との接触（触）があり、接触によって感受（受）があり、感受によって欲望（愛）があり、欲望によって執着（取）があり、執着によって輪廻的な生存（有）があり、輪廻的な生存によって出生（生）があり、出生によって老いと死（老死）という憂い・悲しみ・苦しみ・嘆き・悩みが生ずる。このようにして、すべてのこの苦しみのあつまりが生起することになる。 もっとも、仏教はこうした人間の意識による世界分別認識作用こそが、人間の無明（無知）であり「苦」の元であるゆえ、「我」を滅せよ、「意識」を滅せよ、と説く。元凶は「我思う故に我あり」という人間の驕り高ぶった人間主義・世界観にある。したがって、世界を「我見」でなく「ありのままに」見よ、となるわけだ。ゆえ、ここに東西の「我」対「無我」の図式が浮かび出るわけだが、大事なのは二項対立の形ではなく、「“関係性”という“動態”への認識が共通すること」だ。それは西欧が「範」とするギリシア哲学も、アジアが「なんとなく共有」するインド・中国思想も同じ。全ての二元論は「有無」「表裏」「善悪」「正誤」「陰陽」のように同一事象が含む二面性（多面性というべきだが）を象徴するものでしかない。プラトンは「ヘテロ」を「異」（音）とみなしたが、「ヘテロ」を「異」を含む「多」として「同一」に包含する古代インド・中国思想も「同異」それ自体の認知（感覚的体験）は共通する。要はその事象に対するそれぞれの「態度」（弁別するか包摂するか）の違いであって、どちら側からこれを語るかは「使用言語」によるのではなかろうか。「ことわけ」（言分け・事分け）とはその意で、言語による世界の分節に他ならない。言語は、いわば同一真理・原理への根源的な「態度」を司り、文化を醸成する。ゆえこそ、三善は西欧語と日本語（日本語の複雑さは世界に類がない）の間で取るべき「態度」を「音化」することにその生涯を賭けた。 ここまで来れば、「遠方より無へ」の深甚遠大が見えてこよう。フッサールは時折、「音楽」あるいは「音」それ自体の存在顕現力に言及しているが、こうした嘆息の如き「漏れ」言葉を拾ってゆくと、「あるがまま」の同一地平が現れる。思惟する人（哲人）、あるいは創作家にとって、この世における人間存在（人間のありよう）の彼方・深淵とは、等しく「遠方より無へ」なのだ、と直感されるのではないか。そうしてそれが何より、三善の「音」に現前していることに、粛然とする。 に際立つ「裂け目」置き（『レオス』にも顕著）に現れる三善の「間合い」は、対自というより即自（それ自体として在る）。つまるところ楽音に潜在する志向性を瞬時に掴み我が意識作用（働き）へと引っ張り込む、それら「一気の働き」で、その全体を司り統べるのは彼の「本質直感」だ、というのが私の結論。 ここで「間取り間合い」とは、すでに『王孫不帰』（男声合唱、ピアノと2人の打楽器奏者のための）での能の謡採用時における時空間での響きの配列・按配に現れているもの。計測・計量的な西欧書法とは異なるドラマトゥルギーの気息（息遣い）たる三善書法だ。彼は『ノエシス』をわざわざ定量記譜と断っているが、むしろ、「西欧的定量記譜にはしたけれど」との呟きと私には聞こえる。我がノエシスは、我がノエシスの「本性」を、『レオス』（ギリシア語の変形と流動の意）では「生死合一」ドラマとして、『ノエシス』では「ノエシス」ドラマとしてあからさまにしたわけで、同一路線上。三善解説の最後の一句「それは、いつも、そうしていたことなのかもしれないが。」との嘆息漏れは、まさにそれを物語るようだ。 が、本作を「ノエシス」と名付けた三善の意識（意味付与・言語化・連関）は、彼にとって必須の過程であったことは確かだろう。我が裡なる西欧を俎上に上げてこそ、我が裡なる日本が明らめられもしよう。その意味で、本作は「遠方より無へ」の結節的一瞥であり、その後の創作の一つの参照点となった。 ゆえこそ、翌年の童歌「はないちもんめ」を歌う『詩篇』（1979/混声合唱と管弦楽）に跳べた。 ＊ ＊ ＊ 90年代「交響四部作」連作、『夏の散乱』（1995）『谺（こだま）つり星』（1996/チェロ協奏曲第2番）『霧の果実』（1997）『焉歌・波摘み』（1998）での『谺（こだま）つり星』の独奏チェロや、『焉歌・波摘み』の子守唄の流れもまた、もう一つの「弧」。 そうしてオペラ『遠い帆』がくる。 が、眼差しを大きく遠くひらくなら、「遠方より無へ」とは、文字通り「〜より〜へ」の志向性そのもの。働きそのもの。虹のように天空に架り、見る場所で見え方も異なり、現れ、消え、また現れ、また消え、の「弧」の無限の連なり、命（生死）と等しく、果てない連鎖、果てない架橋、果てない円環なのだ。 迷いにあって発した三善の真言「遠方より無へ」は、ゆえこそ、彼の生涯そのものにかかる果てなき虹の橋梁であった。 私に今、見えるのは、そんな眺め。 さらに。 En passant ― 人も時も通り過ぎる「そのとき何ごとが起ころうと起こるまいと、そこに何ものが残ろうと残るまいと、通り過ぎることそのことが、今の私にはとても美しく見える。」 私に今、聴こえるのは『遠い帆』の「運命という名の神」に選 ばれた六右衛門のこんな声。 「私たちはできるだけのことをした それが受け容れられようと 受け容れられまいと パーデレ それが何だと言うのか 後のことはあなたの愛の神が考えて下さるでしょう。」（『遠い帆』17.帰路） ＊ ＊ ＊ このところ、実存主義だの現象学だの、形而上学に偏ったのは、この時期、三善がそのように「在った」から。 が、そうした抽象論の一方で、彼はその「気息書法」（と今は呼ぼう）あるいは「無空世界」を無論、邦楽器から確実に学びとってもいた。 次回はそこを見よう。 （2026/9/15） 参考資料) items._cn_summary: 日本作曲家三善晃的管弦乐作品《ノエシス》（1978）以定量记谱构建多重乐器群的独立持续与相互参与，融合萨特存在主义与胡塞尔现象学的哲学框架，将意识作用转化为音响与时间的结构。评论从作曲家自述出发，剖析其如何以乐器音的潜在意向性作为素材层，通过异常空想的意识统合作用将碎片整合为整体持续。文中提及2026年8月东京艺剧场的现场演绎，尾高忠明指挥都响的诠释带来冲击，作品被视为《レオス》脉络的延伸，开篇与结尾的大提琴独奏构成核心戏剧张力。评论学术性强，聚焦哲学概念与音乐结构的映射分析。

items.excerpt: 米ミシシッピ出身で東京在住のディープ・ハウサーによるライフワーク・シリーズ第5弾。〈アンチAI〉をテーマにピアノやシンセ、リズムマシーンなど、すべてハードウェアのみで制作され、文字通り長尺のハウス・トラック6つで構成されている。削ぎ落とされた無機質な電子音のなかに有機的な柔らかさや温もりが感じられ、アトモスフェリックでドリーミーな聴後感が印象的だ。

items._cn_summary: 东京在住的米西西比出身制作人Will Long推出其生命周期系列第五作，以〈反AI〉为创作主旨，刻意排除任何软件工具，全程使用钢琴、合成器与节奏机等硬件设备完成六首长篇house曲目。制作理念强调人手操控的温度与机器逻辑之间的张力，在精简的无机电子音里注入有机柔软感，营造出氛围化的梦幻听感。整体追求减法美学，以持续铺展的纹理和缓慢呼吸的结构取代传统house的节奏驱动力，适合沉浸式聆听而非舞池消费。专辑在制作方法论层面提出明确立场，即对当下算法生成音乐的反思，但其音乐语言仍基本停留在deep house与ambient的交汇地带，未在声音设计或结构层面实现更激进的突破。

items._cn_summary: 这是WILLOW乐队第八张专辑，距离前作仅半年便面世。相较于前作近乎一人独立完成的状态，本作转为完整的乐队编制制作，邀请长期合作的克里斯·格雷蒂全面协助，并特别邀请日裔乐手梅·西蒙斯参与录制。作品以先锋爵士摇滚为骨架，融入自由即兴的爵士元素，同时展现出强烈的艺术性与精神性追求。整体制作体现出不受拘束的实验态度，将摇滚乐队的编制与爵士的即兴逻辑结合，呈现出融合跨界色彩的声音探索。专辑在风格跨度与制作深度上有所拓展，但因乐评原文仅为简短介绍，缺乏对具体曲目编排与声音细节的深入描述，信息的丰富程度有限。

items.body: Artwork by Natasha at Aza Nizi Maza And we are back after the summer break with a new episode of UFN. I wish Ukraine could have had a bit of a break as well, but far from it. Ballistic missile attacks have only intensified, while Kramatorsk and Slovyansk increasingly resemble ghost towns. This month we introduce several new voices to the UFN universe, including Aircraft, whom I had the pleasure of meeting in Berlin back in June; Bey O Bey from Kyiv, praising the level of organisation in smaller cities such as Khmelnytskyi and Vinnytsia; TRANCEDÆNCE, referencing the work of Mark Fisher; and Соня Хедекель [Sofiia Khedekel], who is starting to forget what life was like before the full-scale invasion in Kharkiv. Furthermore, Roksana Smirnova and Misha Kalinin imagine the moment after the war ends in Tallinn, and Forma Formanta, in Kyiv, discusses freedom. We are also very pleased to reconnect with old friends Bohdan Stupak, Fedir Tkachov and Lu Joyce, as well as the Sumy-based label Bondeni through Kateryna Pavlovska, all talking to us about their new releases. There’s a big crop of new music, including a double fundraisier by Side-Line Magazine and releases by Alexander Stratonov, Alla Zagaykevych, Ambiotik, Corn Wave, Cryptic Chorus, Decorodi, Doctor Bugg, Horizon Resonances, Khladna Landscape, Kotra, Mootney, Motorpig, Neroba, Oleksii Podat, Peshka, Piriinka, Regina Collage, Ross Khmil, Sasha Chemerov & Hidden Element, Tetiana Khoroshun, v4w.enko, Valentin Silvestrov, ХЖВИ, Ніщо, Vøvk, КАТ, Serhii Litinskyi, DJ POPS and 58918012. In the mix section, we have new sets by Vlad Fisun, Bogdan Zaiets, Ecce Lizard, Reshat and Khrystyna Kirik. In the viewing room, we have videos by Natalia Tsupryk, Ignea, Vera Logdanidi and Zavoloka, alongside a new documentary by Suspilne about Ukrainian children being adopted in Italy under the guise of the international principle of “the best interests of the child”. We also feature a DJ set by Ro_Ma 4E (Roman Cherkas), a veteran who took up DJing thanks to EnterDJ and performed at one of the Czech Republic’s most popular festivals, Colours of Ostrava, back in July. And to finish proceedings, a set by Vlad Fisun. Daryna But first, this month’s Resonance FM podcast features Daryna, a 16-year-old girl from Kharkiv, talking about the art studio Aza Nizi Maza, founded by Mykola Kolomyets in 2012 and working creatively with children with disabilities and those on the autism spectrum. The studio has continued to operate throughout the full-scale invasion, becoming both a haven for creativity and a reference point for foreign journalists seeking to understand life in Kharkiv. During our conversation, we discussed the studio’s ethos, the language issue, and what everyday life is like for schoolchildren in Kharkiv, where classes are now conducted online and students meet physically once a week, with only a limited number actually attending in person. Aza Nizi Maza Studio Tracklist: headachee – хедейк Соня Хедекель – Унісон SadSvit – Той, хто пісню грав REGINA COLLAGE – Горизонт ХЖВИ – Они все nearr – Календар СТРУКТУРА ЩАСТЯ – Лесбіянство (не) модно Zhadan, Ojra, Kiritchenko – Чорнотроп Dirtbag Loris – Праска   JULY 21, 2026 – BERLIN photo by @yaroslavstorchak Aircraft Your latest album, Тигролови, marks a return to singing entirely in Ukrainian, and even its visual identity draws on the work of the celebrated Ukrainian folk artist Mariya Prymachenko, whose paintings have become powerful cultural symbols in recent years. Before discussing the record itself, could you introduce yourself to our readers and tell us about your musical background? What led you to start making music as Aircraft, and why did returning to the Ukrainian language—and to these distinctly Ukrainian visual and cultural references—feel important for this album? Hi, I started Aircraft 15 years ago as a side lo-fi project which eventually grew up to what it is now. My background was mainly grunge then garage-punk music, I played in several bands, including Buzzmonster, Martiansdoitbetter, The Dontpaniks. I just fell in love with delays in reverbs at some point and switched to more postpunk sound. Ukrainian was always big for me, I was listening mainly to Ukrainian or Western music. And before pro-russian dictator Yanukovich – Ukrainian was very big in underground. For example in 2008-2010 we were singing mainly Ukrainian. Then russia took it from us, pouring billions in propaganda of russian culture. Before Ukrainian was developing quite rapidly. So now it is a third renesanse on my memory of Ukrainian language – 90’s then 2000s then 2014-now. So as an artist i feel responsibility to work with Ukrainian audience, also exporting our culture, and cultural code abroad. Your lyrics often rely on deceptively simple images—night, forests, birds, wire, winter—that gradually accumulate emotional weight without ever becoming overtly symbolic. “Мавĸа” (Mavka) draws on Ukrainian folklore while remaining firmly grounded in the emotional reality of the present, while “Люди” (People) and “Зона” (The Zone) evoke displacement through remarkably economical language. How do songs usually begin for you? Do they emerge first from words, melodies, or atmospheres? I think from memories, by actualising them we create future and hope. That what my music is about. The album repeatedly returns to the idea of waiting. In “Гаю Час” (Killing Time), waiting becomes almost a state of existence, while “Навĸоло Ніч” (Night All Around) transforms the night into a space where time seems suspended altogether. These songs avoid political slogans, yet the war is present in every silence and every hesitation. Was it important for you to write about the psychological consequences of war rather than documenting events directly? I don’t agree that it doesn’t have political slogans, I say, “I will never forgive the world when the war is over”. Which means the passiveness of western politicians, often loyal to russia, fossil fuels dependancy instead of protection etc. Tons of hypocrisy. That is quite political I think. What does it mean for you to be Ukrainian and if you had to pick a film, novel, artwork, building, dish, song, album, and meme that best represents Ukraine for you at present what would you choose? Emm. I don’t like this question. I would rather answer what does it mean to be a Ukrainian artist. It is picking the hardest themes to work with. Developing fast, by accepting harsh reality as it is. Struggling being “too authentic” in the standartized and refined European industry. A lot of distributors, streaming platforms and music businesses in general still recognise the post soviet map as one environment, which is ridiculous, since it hasn’t existed for 40 years. Which smells like chauvinism to me. All in all I think there is still quite a lot of that in Europe. As a Ukrainian and a Ukrainian artist I faced it a lot. And we now pay for our recognition a very high price. However, I always see bright lights of hope here and there, and your project is one of them. So thank you!   AUGUST 12, 2026 – KYIV Bohdan Stupak Hi Bohdan, when we spoke back in 2024, you said that the full-scale invasion had made you realise you needed “a stronger voice” for your story to be heard, and much of your work at the time—war.datapoints, Voices of War, “air raid siren is over”—dealt quite directly with the sonic reality of war. Since then, book of sorrow and a place in memories seem to turn inward, towards beauty, memory, loss and contemplation. What has changed for you over these two years, both personally and as an artist? Is this retreat from explicitly war-related material a consequence of the fatigue you describe in the notes to book of sorrow, or does it represent a more fundamental change in what you now want music to do? Surely, there is fatigue present. Nobody expected that the war would drag on for more than 4 years. And one cannot stay constantly alert for such a long time. But also, a lot of things happened in my personal life. Getting to know loss, grief. And the art was always a great therapeutic way to process such strong feelings. But most importantly, although now I’m dealing with more “neutral” subjects, people from other countries still ask me about what it is like being a Ukrainian nowadays and ask me a lot about life in Ukraine. So I guess, working with such universal topics still allows me to raise the voice I dreamed of, although in softer ways. Back then, circumstances had forced you to leave your guitar in Kyiv, and you told me that you hoped eventually to bring organic sounds back into your music. book of sorrow almost feels like the fulfilment of that wish: the entire record was made from a single guitar, processed until it can resemble horns, strings or an ensemble, while drawing on Baroque harmony and the European classical tradition. Why did you impose this restriction on yourself, particularly after working so extensively with SuperCollider, algorithms, field recordings and data? It is not like I imposed the restriction. It’s rather that I was so mesmerised with the sound that I got, that I felt that nothing else was needed! Of course, with “a place in memories”, I had to move further and incorporate this type of sound into my entire system of program-generated textures. And did rediscovering the guitar change the way you thought about composition? I wouldn’t say that it was a dramatic change, but rather a gradual process that happened over the years. With my first project “fractions” I explored the entire sonic field with the means of numbers. But when “grammars” arrived, I felt I had to find the link between beauty and the algorithm. So now, when I have a guitar at my disposal, I have another powerful instrument I can augment the algorithm with. There is an interesting progression from book of sorrow to a place in memories. On the former you write about seeking beauty as nourishment during a period of exhaustion, although war inevitably remains present beneath the music; on the latter, memory itself becomes the subject, beginning with your recollection of the Black Sea in 2017 and the recognition that an occupied part of Ukraine now exists for you less as a geographical place than as “a certain point in the past”. How do you distinguish memory from nostalgia here? It’s a great word “nostalgia”. I think it was the missing word that would neatly describe the music when I was writing one-sheet for it. And I think it’s great that this is nostalgia, not just memory, as listeners seek emotion, not the documentality. When a place still exists physically but has become inaccessible through occupation, does remembering it alter the meaning of both place and time? It is a hard question. On the one hand, the place would be special anyways because of that special time we had there, which we can never bring back. But on the other hand, I feel bitterness every time I think that those places are not only physically inaccessible now but also plundered (like Askania Nova natural reserve). In 2024 you spoke about how quickly the human mind can adapt to almost anything, to the point that war can acquire the texture of ordinary life; you also chose Vasyl Stefanyk’s The Stone Cross as the work that best represented Ukraine for you, partly because of its protagonist’s relationship to the land and the labour invested in it. a place in memories returns repeatedly to landscape—“endless fields”, “horizon”, “orchards”, “mist”, “old porch”, “rings on the water”, “fireflies”—but now landscape seems inseparable from absence. Has your idea of home, land and what it means to be Ukrainian changed since our previous conversation? Not at all. The paradox is that although the land is a focal point of the “Stone cross”, it is far less landscape-centered than “a place in memories”. In the book, the land is rather a medium that bears the fruit of a person’s hard labor. In modern-day interpretation, it could be anything that represents that hard, relentless labor to make something out of this life. For instance, a bottle of olive oil. There was an anecdote back in the early days of full-scale invasion, that russians who marauded houses in Bucha found a bottle of olive oil, and as they had never seen it before, they decided that this was some sort of fancy liquor, and attempted to drink it! They didn’t consider applying their work to improve their lives and afford better nutrition, but instead they chose to travel almost half of the globe to ruin other people’s lives instead. Ukrainians are the opposite of it, which can be seen not only in powerful gestures, but also in small, cozy, convenient things. And after more than four years of full-scale war, are you still able to imagine these places in the future, rather than primarily remembering them in the past? Sure. From time to time, I think of those sunlit fields, bus stations in small towns, buildings of agricultural factories standing tall across the steppe, cozy villages, and of course sea. I can definitely envision my wife and me traveling there again, but this time together with our son. Although, as memorising those places now is rather nostalgia than memory, visions of such a future are rather a dream than a plan.   AUGUST 12, 2026 – ODESA Lu Joyce Looking at your recent records together, there seems to be a clear evolution rather than a sudden change of direction. Mastermind, made from recordings dating from 2022–24, remains largely rooted in ambient, drone and electroacoustic texture; Symbols of Escapism begins introducing more defined beats and moves between ambient, IDM and techno; and now Amphibia commits much more fully to dub techno. Do you hear these three records as stages in the same process? What gradually drew you from the freer, more textural music of Mastermind towards rhythm, repetition and eventually the dub structures of Amphibia? As for the evolution , it’s more in certain techniques and details. I didn’t plan to make a specifically dub techno album with Amphibia; it’s a random selection of tracks that share a common theme of water and something from a different realm of presence. That’s probably where the similarity with dub techno reference points lies. Although there is a micro sauna and ambient in the track “Expo.” I think it’s inspired by the works of Romeo Poirier. As for the last three albums and their connection, they’re more like three different mes that live in an agreement with each other. Many of Gurdjieff’s “I”s come to mind, but this is a different multiplicity. I would call it a multiplicity of vectors. When we first spoke in 2022, you said that tuning was “the heart of a track”, while other pieces could emerge from the detailed treatment of random sound events. I wonder how that approach translates into Amphibia, where tracks such as “Omni Dub”, “Orchid Dub” and “Dolphine” seem much more concerned with pulse, repeated chords, bass and delay. When constructing these pieces, what now comes first: tuning and atmosphere, as it did in your earlier work, or rhythm and the manipulation of space? Yes, that’s absolutely right. In Amphibia, the basis is rhythmic structures, because the amphibian doesn’t lie on the bottom for long; it’s always wandering somewhere, wandering strangely. But I’ve been a real fan of the Chain Reaction label for the last year, and I even started collecting their vinyl records, even though I don’t have a turntable lol. perhaps subconsciously this began to influence the sound. It also seems significant that Amphibia has appeared on Insectorama. Back in 2022, before you were making explicitly dub-oriented records, you already mentioned the “constant support from the dub producers community”. How did your relationship with Insectorama and Markus Masuhr develop, and why did the label feel like the right destination for this particular record? Masuhr also mastered Amphibia and created its artwork—how much did that exchange contribute to the final identity of the album? Strangely enough, dub has become my ally, even though I’d previously ignored the genre and avoided it. I discovered the work of the Insectorama label by chance, but I remember listening to their releases all night over a bottle of wine and being struck by how interesting the label was, so I wanted to send them a demo. I also like their artwork and limited edition discs. Markus Masuhr also did a very good job mastering the tracks and writing the descriptions. He created a whole legend for the album. In 2022 you told me that you no longer wanted to look at the Black Sea because it had become “the sea that is at war”; when I met you in Odesa in 2024, you were rehearsing with Rudnic Ore at More Music Club. What is life in Odesa like for you now, and what has changed since those encounters? There is an intriguing progression here too: Symbols of Escapism already suggests the desire to move elsewhere mentally, while Amphibia is saturated with water, from its title and “Dolphine” to its imagery of pressure waves, liquid galaxies and cosmic oceans. Is there a connection between this imagined aquatic space and your changing relationship with the actual sea surrounding Odesa—and, more broadly, has living through these years changed what you now want music to provide: documentation, escape, abstraction, or something else? Odesa remains my friend and a place of creative enthusiasm. The Black Sea remains a living entity with an ancient spirit. I always communicate with it. Amphibia is an even more distant place—more precisely, a creature that leads to deeper places, and they are imbued with love, despite the strangeness of some of the compositions. If Symbols of Escapism was an escape, then Amphibia is a born essence and ally that, through dub waves, leads to metaphysical depths—to oneself.   AUGUST 14, 2026 – KYIV Bey O Bey I’m Sashko Bey. Bey is actually my surname, and at first my nickname “bey o bey” seemed a bit funny to me, but over time it turned into something I’m known by. I like it, and everyone likes it, so I’m happy with it. I live in Kyiv, but I was born in Donetsk region — I moved here because of the war, back in 2014. Since childhood I’ve listened to a huge amount of music. For me, listening was almost like an analysis, a real pleasure — I was always more interested in listening to music, figuring out the artist, the genres they work in, and so on, than watching a film, and that’s stayed with me to this day. As for my musical background: my friends and I used to organize parties, and that’s where I played my first DJ set, sometime around 2017–2018. Then in 2019 I joined a school called Kultura Zvuka to learn how to play vinyl, under a teacher named Rustam. Fun fact — over the past few years we’ve actually played four b2b sets together, and it was incredible every time. My friend Denys, with whom I later founded Terms of Groove, also signed up for that vinyl course — I joined him, and it turned out to be a great decision, because from that point on I fell in love with music on records. I think I’ve been collecting vinyl since around 2019. As for what first drew me to electronic music and vinyl, and how my approach as a DJ took shape — I was already playing music and buying tracks before the vinyl course, mostly house, tech house, minimal. Back then I was really into Romanian minimal, and that's actually what I started my record collection with — Denys and I played a lot of Romanian minimal together. Even now, so many years later, I still put those records on and enjoy them; they still sound great. As for how my approach as a DJ developed — I think I looked a lot at other people, how they did things, and tried to do what was being done in Kyiv at the time. There was always this internal tug-of-war between what was happening around me and what I actually liked myself, and I’d look for some kind of compromise. It’s only now that I’ve reached the point where I play what I want, and I don’t care what anyone else thinks. I collected records, and they were completely all over the place: I started with Romanian minimal, but then I picked up ambient, some house-leaning stuff, broken beat, and more. Gradually I realized I didn’t want to limit myself in any way — I wanted to play everything I wanted to play. I wouldn’t say my sets were ever especially one-note — I always tried to keep them varied. A lot changed when I discovered Discogs and started spending hours there every day. It’s like a door opening onto a collection of millions of records from different years and genres — you can dig and dig endlessly. After that discovery I started playing mostly older music. These days it’s roughly a mix of 80% old and 20% new, more or less. Of course I still buy new releases too. As for being one of the founders of Terms of Groove and now a resident at Brukxt, and how my musical identity has changed — at first, together with the guys, we founded Terms of Groove in a format built mostly around house-adjacent genres: house, tech house, minimal, progressive. I always loved broken music and collected a lot of it, but I’d only sprinkle it into house sets here and there. At some point I decided to try playing a set made up entirely of broken records, since I’d accumulated so many of them at home. It turned out to be a fully broken set. It was great, something completely new for me. Over time I got noticed and was invited to become a resident at Brukxt club — and I dove even deeper into broken music from there. As for how my identity changed — a lot of broken records got added to my usual house collection, sometimes even darker ones, sometimes just really driving, high-energy ones. And overall my performances changed too, in the sense that when you’re playing broken music, it’s active, and you just want to jump around behind the decks And honestly, in recent years I don’t limit myself at all anymore — not by genre, not by tempo, not by era. I play what I want and how I want, and that’s the whole fun of it Looking back at 2025, you described it as an especially productive year, with performances across Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. You’ve played at venues such as Brukxt, Closer, Keller, Abo Records, Brave! Factory, and also in Kharkiv at Some People. How would you describe the character of Kyiv’s electronic music scene today, and how does it compare with Kharkiv or other cities you’ve played in? Despite the war, does each city still retain its own musical identity? Yes — over New Year’s I sat down and looked at how many shows I’d played in 2025, and I was genuinely shocked. I traveled to a lot of cities across the country, and it was a great experience. It really was a productive year — I was playing almost every week, and I gave up a lot of other things to make that happen. But it was worth it. As for how I’d describe Kyiv’s electronic scene today, and how it compares to Kharkiv or other cities I’ve played in — Kyiv’s scene is, without question, a level above the others, first and foremost in scale. In terms of quality it also wins out almost everywhere. For example, I love that in Kyiv, wherever you walk into on a Friday, there’s good music playing, and very often the place is packed — that’s a genuinely great sign. There are a lot of really good DJs in Kyiv; it feels like every second person collects records. The competition is fierce, but it’s inspiring, and overall it’s a great thing. I want to highlight Kharkiv — the guys there built Some People, and they’ve also brought the Kultura Zvuka approach into a club format; there's another club as well, and overall the electronic music culture in Kharkiv is moving in a really good direction. I genuinely loved playing there. I also want to say again — I was genuinely struck by the level of organization, the level of everything, in the smaller cities like Khmelnytskyi and Vinnytsia. Of course the communities there are much smaller, and it takes an enormous amount of work to get people to understand what this culture is really about. I’m grateful to the people building that scene there — without them, none of what exists now would exist. The problem I see in other cities is that there’s no money, not enough people, and it’s very hard to grow it. As for whether each city still retains its own musical identity despite the war — I think it’s even harder for the smaller cities: places and parties like that exist on much shakier ground there. Since the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s electronic music community has continued to grow in remarkable ways. From your perspective, how has the scene changed over the past three years? Has the role of DJs, promoters, and clubs evolved, and what gives you optimism about where Ukrainian electronic music is heading? Before the war I wasn’t that integrated into this electronic community, so my perspective can really only speak to how things look now — specifically from a DJ’s point of view. What I can say is that there are a lot of DJs now, and to get noticed you need to stand out musically somehow, stand out visually somehow, or have good connections so you get booked somewhere and get seen there. There are actually a lot of really good DJs who struggle to promote themselves — they’ve built incredible music collections but rarely get to play, because that takes a promoter. Overall we now have a huge number of DJs of our own. Promoters and clubs, of course, have it very hard during the war, because there are shellings, and it happens that Saturday is a day of mourning right when you have foreign artists booked, or a big party you’ve spent months preparing for — and it all gets cancelled. The war keeps making its own adjustments. But I’m honestly amazed that despite all these circumstances, you sometimes walk into a party and just lose yourself in it completely — it’s like a different world. It’s incredible that during the war there’s a place you can go where everything is always good. That’s genuinely amazing. What gives me optimism about where Ukrainian electronic music is heading — when I play music and see people smiling, enjoying it, and then someone comes up afterward and tells me it was great, that gives me a good mood and the motivation to keep going. As a multi-genre selector, your sets move freely across styles, eras, and tempos rather than staying within a single genre. What do you look for when building a set? Is there a narrative or emotional arc you’re trying to create, or do you prefer to let the crowd and the records themselves shape the journey? First and foremost, I start from the venue where I’m playing. Second is the slot — what time it is. Then a kind of picture forms in my head of roughly what I could play at that time, and after that I just go about my day, walking around, and a thought pops into my head: “maybe this record”; — and if I have it, I add it to a list of records that would be fun to play in that slot. By a few days before the show you’ve got a big list of records, and you just sit down, go through them, and throw them in the bag. And something good usually comes out of that — that’s roughly how it works. I never buy records for a specific set — I buy records regardless of circumstances, just all the time. When I need to pull something together for a specific show, I simply pick from my collection. As for an emotional arc — in about 90% of cases it’s some kind of positive emotion. I want my music to bring out positivity in people, smiles, a certain simplicity. I’m not one of those DJs who plays super, super deep music — at least that’s how I see myself; someone else might see it differently. Looking back over the past four years, are there any Ukrainian electronic — or indeed any Ukrainian — albums that you feel have captured the experience of the full-scale invasion or contemporary life in Ukraine in a particularly meaningful way? What makes those records stand out to you? One of the first things that comes to mind is the work of Si Process. I’ve seen him play live several times, including a solo show, and discovering his music during the war has been a real highlight for me. Finally, what does it mean to be Ukrainian today? And if you had to introduce someone unfamiliar with Ukraine through a single film, artwork, meme, traditional dish, song, building or monument, and album, what would you choose — and why? Being Ukrainian today means trying to live and enjoy life despite a huge number of obstacles and a huge number of hard moments, while still holding on to your identity and taking comfort in the fact that the people around you are the same as you — Ukrainians who understand you without needing to finish a sentence. If it’s about a song, or where to send someone to listen to Ukrainian music — I’d point to the YouTube channel in.rec_kyiv, which records sets by Ukrainian DJs. If you don’t know what to listen to, you can just open it and dive in — there are sets recorded in some really cool locations, like a vinyl fair or a clothing store. As for a film — two recent ones stood out to me: the documentary Okean Elzy: Stormwatch (Океан Ельзи: Спостереження Шторму;), and the film about Nazariy Yaremchuk, Yaremchuk: The Incomparable World of Beauty; (Яремчук: Незрівнянний світ краси). And there’s also a great book — A History of Ukrainian Rave; (Історія українського рейву) published by Book-ye — I’d recommend it.   AUGUST 17, 2026 – DNIPRO Live at the Construction Festival TRANCEDÆNCE Hi Oleksandr, thank you for joining us. Let’s jump right into it. Your debut, 0ne, was built from first-take improvisations with no post-production, and you described the act of making it as a trance in which the creator briefly becomes united with the creation. How did you arrive at this way of working, and what was your musical background before TRANCEDÆNCE? Has improvisation remained central to the project, or has your relationship with composition changed since then? Before TRANCEDÆNCE I was mainly focused on my first project, Cynpym. I’d always dreamed of making music, and under that alias I released whatever I felt confident enough to put my name behind. I was still learning FL Studio and had no real plan — mostly hip-hop beats and my own rapping, sometimes vaporwave and even krautrock. A real shift came when I started writing music with the structure of more rave-oriented genres. I was under the heavy influence of the Odesa underground club scene at the time, which gave me a completely different sense of how music could be experienced — the idea of “speakers/acoustics as an instrument,” working with crisp frequencies and timbres.I’d never really listened to much EDM before I started clubbing and got exposed to big sound systems. Before that, I wrote music with more of a rock/pop logic; shifting my focus from compositional structure toward short, repetitive loops that still sound interesting made me appreciate my own music far more, and audiences responded to it too with better feedback and more streams. The project was growing and I started getting some fanbase and developing my own style. From young years I was really into experimental music, so I kept trying to make my music unconventional – sampling avant garde artists, utilizing polyrhythms, building my own kicks out of tom-toms. One of the things I tried was jamming and modulating a sound, then releasing the recording itself as the finished song instead of writing a composition step by step. That later became the whole method behind TRANCEDÆNCE. Originally TRANCEDÆNCE was meant to be an alter ego — it first appeared on a track called Twins where I introduced it as a mysterious collaborator; I even talked to people online in character, with its own name and backstory (the illusion didn’t survive long though — I got caught using the name while playing Minecraft with friends). I’d originally intended TRANCEDÆNCE to sound closer to post-trance / SoundCloud-core / nightcore, scenes I’d gotten into after COVID, chasing something more spiritual and hauntological — but it didn’t fit the way I was used to making music. Then, in one sessionі, I’ve started just modulating the shit out of a short synth loop on one of the new VST and decided to just record it. The process of turning the knobs felt almost ritualistic. When I listened back, the recording had everything I’d been chasing for months, so I recorded a couple more sessions the same way and put them up on SoundCloud the same day, this time under TRANCEDÆNCE. I was genuinely surprised by the results — for the first time, I felt I’d made something complete that represented my own ideas and emotions. I realized it belonged to a completely different discourse than what I’d been aiming for — much closer to noise music and avant-garde practice than anything else. Less than a week after making music this way for the first time, I asked to perform at a local experimental-arts event, sent demos to Ereh Saw, who was organizing it, and got approved. Only two weeks separated the first time I tried free improvisation from my first-ever live performance — and it went well: I improvised alongside a performance artist who was wrapping her naked body in adhesive tape. The audience loved it, and the feedback told me I was on the right track. While recording 0ne I was completely absorbed in this new method — I wanted to demonstrate its possibilities, find its limits, and understand what it meant.I didn’t know yet that it would become the core of the whole project. In some ways it still hasn’t changed: my most recent album, Dnipro City Guardian, is structurally identical to my debut — one synth, one short loop, notes that never change through the track, no post-production beyond mastering, one channel. But where 0ne dwells inside the method itself, almost like an essay film, DCG just utilizes it as an instrument to tell about many different themes and concepts. Free improvisation is still the core medium for TRANCEDÆNCE, though my lens has shifted a lot since the debut. I don’t always limit myself to one channel anymore — I recently wrote a piece for an octophonic installation where each speaker carried the signal from a different synth I was modulating live. But it’s still trance at heart: I pick patches that feel interesting, give them one or two notes, loop them, hit record, and start modulating. Some of those presets I could work with forever and get a different result every time, but I always prefer to release the first take — it keeps the raw energy and the surprise of discovering where a sound can go. This philosophy works amazingly for live performances – most of the time I just need to choose a patch that has a lot of potential to mutate in interesting ways. it’s never about rehearsal, always about reading the room and getting into a flow state where I steer the sound toward a story I don’t fully know myself until I’m in it. Some projects have more anchors — compositional, conceptual, dramaturgical — but the core stays the same: a MIDI loop and my hands on the synth’s parameters. Time seems to have been an important idea in your work from the beginning. The text accompanying Trip Reserved rejects linear time in favour of a “reservoir” in which past and future events coexist, while later records increasingly seem occupied by memory, spectres and particular places. How has your understanding of time changed since you made Trip Reserved in 2021, especially after the full-scale invasion? I believe what changed is not my overall understanding and feeling of time, which I find quite transpersonal, but my focus about that. I still feel myself quite dissociated from time and often I find myself in situations where I am able to feel and understand myself and what is happening around me only in retrospect, or to make choices that would only make sense in a context I’ll get in a future, so nothing much changed there. But my attention now goes toward therapy, humanism, and political action within that same configuration of time. I believe a lot of people today experience the stress of living in a time in its totalitarian manifestation and it’s important to do something about it, to fight for emancipation of time. Capitalism and authoritarianism don’t only make time unbearable — they do the same to our bodies, relations with nature, language, geography and many other basic aspects of our living life – and different people carry different parts of that weight as trauma. Mark Fisher wrote about some of this in Acid Communism, the book he never finished — we only have the introduction, because he took his own life before writing the rest. He argued that we have the capacity to imagine and use time in far more creative ways than capitalism allows. But when the political, economic, and psychological situation gets as bad as it has for so many people — especially in Ukraine — there’s very little room left to play with time, because so many people are simply fighting to survive. When things are this hard, I think the most important thing is to help each other: to remind each other that our dreams are still real, and to feel empathy for other people’s struggles even when we’re luckier or more successful ourselves. So when I work with memory, hauntology, and time now, I try to hold onto that. I don’t want the work to turn cynical or apathetic — I want it to open a dialogue, to let listeners find some hope in it, to remind people that a lot of us carry a similar kind of trauma around time. I’d rather not treat that with irony; I’d rather use it as a reference point for what we build next — as a reminder that time can still become beautiful. at нойзщосереди with Музична Шкатулка (left) You recorded “Monad” at Noise Every Wednesday (нойзщосереди) at Otel’ in Kyiv in January 2024. What was that series like from the inside, and what did it mean to have a regular space devoted to noise and experimental music in wartime Kyiv? At a time when people were already surrounded by the unwanted noise of sirens, drones, explosions and generators, did gathering to make and listen to noise acquire a significance beyond simply having somewhere to perform? “Monad” came from one of two performances I did at Noise Every Wednesday (НЩ) — my debut in the capital, and later a collaboration with Музична Шкатулка. Both are still among the best performances of my career. I found the series quite early and fell in love with the concept immediately — I’d been to noise events in Odesa and Dnipro before and always found them the most interesting to watch as an audience member, so the idea of experiencing that regularly in Kyiv was exciting. I got in touch, sent some material, they liked it, and we booked a date almost immediately. Communication was straightforward and open from the start, and every time I dealt with the team I got the sense that the people running it were motivated, genuinely passionate about what they were doing, and honest and friendly with the artists. It was also impressive on a purely organizational level. Soundchecks were fast and painless, the lighting and visuals were excellent, the sound and monitoring were spectacular, and the tech rider was met in full — if something was missing, they’d always find a solution to make the performance feel complete. As an artist in Ukraine you’re pretty much guaranteed at least one small crisis at venues of a much bigger scale, so having everything taken care of by a project that screamed DIY was genuinely inspiring to say the least. The philosophy of the series helped as much as the organization. Every artist — whether it was their first time on stage or they were a veteran of the scene — got the same level of attention. That’s one of the most beautiful things about НЩ: at almost every show there’d be someone playing their first-ever set alongside “legends” of the Ukrainian underground. At my first performance there, Timur Dzhafarov (aka John Object) publicly premiered his new project, Група Б. At the time I saw Timur as one of the most important musicians in Ukraine, so being able to talk to him and get his feedback was both an honor and a real opportunity. НЩ felt like a place built on non-hierarchy and solidarity, where your status didn’t matter and people from different backgrounds were treated as equals. The other thing that stood out was how liberating it felt that the audience had almost no fixed expectations. It felt like you were allowed to do anything, as long as it wasn’t boring — which meant nobody was anxious about “failing.” It gave artists a green light to try things they’d always wanted to attempt but never had a safe space for. I never did anything especially extreme there myself, but just knowing I could was already freeing as an artist. I once talked about this with Vadym Oliinykov, one of the people behind the project, and he told me something like: “It’d be great if you did something crazy — but keep in mind we don’t have an age restriction, so if you decide to get naked in front of people, we won’t be able to help you with the cops if someone reports it.” Honestly, that’s about the best mindset I can imagine for experimental music. Often the genre tags on the poster mattered more than the artist’s name — you’d go just to hear someone play a harsh noise wall or a lowercase set. For that reason, I think НЩ will end up being important as an archive of Ukrainian musical avant-garde on its own. It was open to everyone, and I think a lot of artists who are, or will become, culturally significant had their start or a key moment there. I’d like to think it will eventually mean as much to Ukrainian underground music as Novaya Scena does now, but that will take time — and it’s a shame that not every show was filmed before НЩ got its own YouTube channel, because I think each of those performances will matter for anyone researching Ukrainian post-war experimental music in the future. I never lived in Kyiv while НЩ was running, so I can’t claim to have seen the whole picture, especially once the events started getting more attention. But it made me want to move there — I wanted to help however I could, and I was told I’d be welcome to keep developing my project within it. I was invited a couple more times before the series ended and couldn’t make it, mostly because I was sure it would just keep going. I hope the community finds a way to self-organize and continue what НЩ started, and the values it brought into the Ukrainian post-war underground. There are still radical music events happening in Kyiv, but none of them feel quite as inclusive. I still hope for some kind of resurgence — the ideas behind НЩ worked perfectly from 2023 to 2025, and I think they’d still work now. But it’s worth remembering it wasn’t just good timing or the underground zeitgeist after the full-scale invasion — Vadym, Kseniia, Misha, and Pavlo worked incredibly hard to make it happen. Your recent work invites a hauntological reading: Dnipro City Guardian contains a track called “Haunt of Kaminya”, while your music repeatedly returns to spectres, loops, memory and distorted temporalities. Mark Fisher famously associated hauntology with futures that were once imagined but never arrived. Does that idea make sense in Ukraine, where an anticipated future was not simply “lost” through cultural stagnation but violently interrupted by invasion? And is there a danger of aestheticising very real ghosts and absences when talking about Ukrainian culture in hauntological terms? I see hauntology less as a fixed thematic or aesthetic lens and more as a genuinely modern discipline that’s still being worked out — which means it can develop in a lot of directions. Interest in working with memory is growing right now, Fisher’s ideas included, and inevitably some of that will romanticize trauma while some of it goes cynical. That kind of recuperation happens to most good ideas eventually, so it’s a risk I try to stay aware of. I don’t think the idea only makes sense in Ukraine now — I think the war has accelerated it to an extreme speed, which means we suddenly have a lot of new material and new angles to work with. Fisher’s original focus was roughly about the decay of the welfare state and the rise of neoliberalism; the Ukrainian context gives us something more anti-colonial and less Euro-centered. You’re right that a lot of what we’ve lost here comes from actual, literal destruction and violence, not slow decay. Until recently, Ukrainian hauntology was mostly about things that had already been haunted for a long time — the Soviet past, the annexation of Crimea. Now people are experiencing these spectres of time at a much faster pace. One day your commute to work is ordinary; the next day it’s changed forever because a building along the route was hit overnight. It’s not only about the horror of that — you start asking smaller, stranger questions too: what will replace this? why was it even here? how do we want to remember this place — do we even want to? what does it mean that I miss this past? A lot of people are already nostalgic for the first months of the war, the first blackouts. There’s a growing pull toward more conventional hauntological gestures — artists sampling Ukrainian pop from the 2000s, grieving lost national futures against the futures Russia tried to promise us instead. Stalker 2 is a good example of how the discourse has shifted since the invasion — the relationship to lost futures there is much more contradictory and tangled than the classic version, closer to how I think Ukrainian collective memory actually works now. We can’t separate ourselves from these missing meanings — not just ideas about a better past or future, but ideas about what being Ukrainian even is. We still need to fight for our present and build a future, but these lost futures and broken pasts have become part of the cultural fabric for a lot of Ukrainians, so I think there’s real, useful work to do with them — using older hauntological tools and building new ones. My own practice has become more centered on hauntology over the last couple of years — “Missing Sounds” among other pieces — and I think I get closer to something meaningful when I try new mediums and methods rather than just sampling or referencing symbols that trigger nostalgia. I’m also finding new ways of noticing my own hauntological code — ghosts I didn’t know I was carrying — in landscape, architecture, sound, local communities, time itself, food, language, products. want those new perspectives to actually do something — to build more promising, more emancipated versions of reality, not just describe the loss. Administration, recorded across 2023, reduces its accompanying text to two words—“drug / politics”—and titles its pieces “Blackout”, “Boise” and “Brothel”. Then Dnipro City Guardian gives us “Taking a Dump at Biennale Restroom”, “DCCC” and “Haunt of Kaminya”. There seems to be a mixture of seriousness, absurdity and private mythology running through these titles. How autobiographical is TRANCEDÆNCE, and how much are you constructing a fictional world around experiences that actually happened? That’s something I think about myself a lot as of recently. I’ve been doing more institutional artist practices and started signing my works with my real name Oleksandr Suprun more frequently, and I’ve realized I can use both names — TRANCEDÆNCE and my real name — more or less interchangeably, depending on what the work needs. From the start of the project I saw TRANCEDÆNCE as whatever musical or sound work I do inside contemporary art and institutional avant-garde music. I still construct and work on the overall artist identity and design of this project to build some cohesive artistic statement. But I see TRANCEDÆNCE as less autobiographical or focused on narrative world-building and much more about conceptual depth and the listener’s own subjective reading — emotional states, psychological associations, that kind of thing. I try to keep things as abstract, vague, and surreal as I can; what a track title looks and sounds like as a combination of letters, or what colors go on the artwork, usually matters more to me than sending any specific message. That said, I can see the project moving toward more worldbuilding or a more unified narrative in specific works, even if that’s not really the focus. With Dnipro City Guardian the album got more personal and specific than anything before it — I wanted to say something about my hometown and its local identity, and for the first time in my career I felt genuinely connected to that. It was a shift for me as much as for the music. I want TRANCEDÆNCE to be open to such dynamics and only be limited to this electroacoustic improvisation praxis I was talking about earlier. The mythos side of things — private mythology, world-building, a constructed persona — is something I work with much more directly under my other alias, Cynpym, which I use for my blog, more conventional music, poetry, graphic work, and my main social presence. I try to keep the two as genuinely separate mindsets and workflows. It’s honestly a challenge right now: TRANCEDÆNCE ended up giving me a functional method and became the direction my career moved in, while Cynpym — which I think of as my main persona, the one I show people most often — has been hard to turn into a complete, larger project. I want to get back to it, because I think it can express things TRANCEDÆNCE simply can’t, but figuring out how to bring what I’ve learned from TRANCEDÆNCE into it, without collapsing the distinction between the two, is an ongoing problem. It might sound like an overly formal thing to worry about, but for me it’s a genuinely interesting one to solve. Photo by Anna Chaika courtesy of Artsvit Gallery Where are you currently based, and how has displacement—or, if you have remained in Ukraine, the transformation of everyday life there—affected the way you make and hear music? More broadly, what does identifying yourself as a Ukrainian artist mean to you now? Is “Ukrainian” primarily a cultural identity, a political position, a lived experience, or something that inevitably enters the sound itself? When the full-scale invasion started I moved back from Odesa to Dnipro, where I still live. For the first months it was mostly about getting all shit together – finding a new job, moving to a new place, making new connections. I didn’t really start thinking about my career again until I went to some of the first post-invasion gigs, some of which I was invited to perform at in late 2022. It was a really strange and transactional period – I see that the community wanted to continue functioning on the same logic and principles as it was before the war, not yet knowing how exactly the scene should transform. I had no idea either – but performing, and reminding myself I was still a musician, mattered a lot. With that mindset I released my second album …&2, which tried to capture that odd, liminal year. I’m not especially proud of it sonically, but I’m glad I made it — it kept me moving forward through a context that had changed completely since February 2022. Time passed and it became more obvious that initial enthusiasm for creating musical events in a pre-war fashion was fading away, at least in Dnipro. The cultural space felt colder and emptier as the first blackouts and Shahed attacks started. I stopped thinking seriously about music for a while — it felt impossible to fit back into the scene without some kind of reinvention. That changed when I went to Kyiv for a 20ft Radio event where Oleksii Podat was playing alongside other experimental and radical artists. Watching a crowd vibe to something that loud and harsh made me think that if I got back into music, there’d actually be an audience for it. That pushed me to put together my first real portfolio, get my old material onto streaming, and start applying to open calls — which eventually led to me being included on the ШЩЦ3 VA compilation, which was a huge deal for me as it got a lot of publications and I admired this label long before making experimental music myself. From there I started more new projects, met more local artists, worked with more Ukrainian art organizations, and did my first residencies. Becoming a direct participant in the Ukrainian underground scene, rather than an outside observer of it, was the biggest change in how I make music. I used to think of my work as representing more global subcultures and networks; now I keep in mind that I represent my local context too, and it’s basically impossible to separate my solo work from the Ukrainian people I’ve collaborated with. Whatever I pick up from elsewhere, I try to bring back and share with the local community as a priority. That’s not always simple — sometimes the local focus feels imposed by institutions, and the community itself keeps shifting and radicalizing politically — but caring about how my work resonates here, and about making something that matters to these specific people, has pushed me to try new mediums, work with new themes, and be more sincere as an artist. As for “Ukrainian” as a label — I think it’s an ongoing process of figuring out what we can be and do, not a fixed or essentialist thing, and I’m wary of romanticizing it. It’s an active practice, where we constantly adapt as a community for the sake of our own survival. It’s a lived experience people gain from cultural code, passport, language, land, contribution to community, etc. A lot of people carry “ukrainity” in different amounts, and for some it grows large enough to shape their whole way of living. Right now, being Ukrainian often means direct action and direct connection — we tend to self-organize without waiting for guidance from above. Turning “Ukrainian” into that kind of flexible, dispersed network, using whatever tools we have, is what we’re doing right now so that we can’t be crushed. Your earlier work repeatedly imagines the future: 0ne refers to technological singularity and “Coming of Age”, while Trip Reserved describes events acquiring meanings only later in life. Are you still able to think about the future in those terms? After more than four years of full-scale war, is imagining a future an artistic necessity, a luxury, an act of resistance—or something that has become almost impossible? I touched on part of this already — to summarize, I still find Mark Fisher’s Acid Communism and Capitalist Realism the most useful frame for thinking about the future, and I’m genuinely glad to see him getting more popular with younger audiences. It’s almost impossible to picture a realistic, positive future right now, but letting yourself start dreaming again feels like the necessary first step toward one. I can’t talk about the future without acknowledging how much has changed over the last few years — new technology, the political climate of USA-China and their world influence, COVID. Since the full-scale invasion, accelerationism feels like the most relevant frame to me globally. Even inside Ukraine, the new shape of drone warfare wasn’t something anyone expected, and its effect on our society and culture is hard to overstate. How we resist, how our trauma is shaped, how we fight and understand this war — all of that is being formed by new technology and new media. The faster we understand how it’s changing us, the better we adapt and the better we do strategically. The accelerationist view can be genuinely frightening given what a lot of theorists predict — especially with the current Trump administration having real roots in Dark Enlightenment thinking. It’s a fact that the tech sector today is largely controlled by people with no real interest in solving the world’s problems or improving people’s lives, and yet the technology keeps developing at full speed regardless. Most political parties, most of the public, even a lot of artists, underestimate or ignore this, while authoritarian regimes are already putting it to use. As an artist I feel a responsibility to engage with this, especially from a Ukrainian angle. I see Ukraine as a place where the future is actively unfolding — not just in terms of which weapons and technologies get used in this war, but in how the war and its outcome will reshape how we understand colonialism, imperialism, and globalism in a world with mass-deployed AI. Ukrainians have been living in that mode for a long time already: we’ve had some of the fastest, cheapest, least censored internet around; most of our schools and universities never fully left remote learning after COVID; we’ve gotten so used to working through blackouts that it’s less disruptive than people might expect. That’s how this society ended up more technologically acknowledged than a lot of much wealthier countries, under some of the worst possible conditions — which I find genuinely inspiring. I think younger Ukrainians are even better positioned to use technology culturally, and if we want to theorize seriously about a better future, we need to pay attention to what they’re actually doing, feeling, and thinking. I doubt many of them care much about experimental or contemporary art in the white-cube highbrow form that still dominates the field. A lot of art mediums and music genres are going to lose relevance fast if we don’t reshape them for younger artists who grew up with technology from birth — otherwise they’ll just go to virtual platforms instead. The same goes for “new money”: IT workers, e-scammers, crypto traders have real potential to become the next Ukrainian elite, so it’s worth starting that conversation now if we want Ukrainian art to have a future worth building. Honestly, these days I see more potential in Instagram Reels brainrot memes than in most institutional art projects, which too often feel technophobic and commodified — not exactly the right configuration for building something better. From debut performance in Odesa Finally, rather than asking you to define Ukraine, could you build a small portrait of the country as it exists for you right now: what book, film, artwork, monument or building, dish, meme, album and individual song best represent contemporary Ukraine—and why? I would choose ‘тсн’ by kissesfromeldar – but honestly, any of their recent releases would be a great fit. That music gives me the most hope about where Ukrainian music is going, and it represents Ukraine the way I want it represented: sincere, vulnerable, queer-coded, post-ironic, cutting-edge, visionary, self-referential, anti-institutional, and still respectful of its roots. I see how this music would be enjoyed equally by Ukrainians and foreigners. I think Ukrainians and foreign listeners can enjoy it equally, for different reasons — for us it’s full of context and references only we’d fully catch, while for people outside Ukraine it just sounds fresh, with very few real equivalents elsewhere. Those are the same qualities I’ve always valued in Svitlana Nianio’s music. kissesfromeldar isn’t based in Ukraine but performs around Europe, which also matters to me — having artists who matter equally to people who stayed and people who left because of the war feels important at a moment when those two groups keep drifting further apart.   SEPTEMBER 2, 2026 – KHARKIV sofiia khedekel Hi Sofiia, could you tell us about your musical background and how Соня Хедекель [Sofiia Khedekel] began as a project? In my own sound, I care about a feeling of real human presence, melancholic haze and the texture I create by layering vocals and guitars. I’m glad you noticed this in your question. I work with music as an emotional space and I’m not really interested in making a quick impression – it’s more important to me that the sound pulls you in and exists as a certain state. If I am not mistaken, you live in Kharkiv, a city that has experienced more than four years of war and remains under frequent attack. How has living there changed since 2022, both personally and as a musician? Is it possible to adapt to that degree of uncertainty, and what are the particular difficulties of trying to write, record, perform and maintain an ordinary cultural life in Kharkiv at the moment? Yes, I live in Kharkiv. Sometimes it is difficult for me to answer the question “how has life changed”, because I feel like I’m starting to forget what life was like before the full-scale invasion, and that scares me. But of course, reality has a strong influence both on the topics I work with and on my approach to creativity in general. In some way, it may be a way for me to process and understand my own emotions and experiences. I have also become much less afraid of imperfection. It feels like, after everything that has happened, it is harder to scare me with things that used to make me feel vulnerable. There is quite a friendly music community in Kharkiv – we try to support each other. At the same time, it is quite small, as many people have left, so it can be difficult to find venues and people with whom you can create something together and move in the same direction. Of course, reality also affects the technical side of making music. For example, I recorded “Незупинно” during a period of severe power cuts after russian attacks. During the day I would go to a café to work, and in the evening, while I had a few hours of electricity at home, I would charge my laptop and record music in Ableton until the battery ran out. I did this sitting in the kitchen by candlelight. I think one day I will remember that period as something surreal. While writing the answer to this question, I remembered how I used to wait for the explosions to stop before starting to record vocals. At the time, I didn’t even think much about it. Now I realize how abnormal our reality has become. There is an interesting tension between your two recent singles. In “Незупинно” you describe the desire for an “emotional escape from reality” while remaining anxiously attached to it; in “Unison”, home becomes something you can find through trust and mutual understanding with another person. The city itself becomes almost weightless as everything seems to dissolve around the two people. Are these songs connected for you? Has your understanding of what “home” means changed through the experience of living in Kharkiv during the war? Yes, these songs are definitely connected – for me, they are two stages of how I am processing everything that is happening. “Незупинно” is probably about accepting that sometimes I simply can’t cope. In Ukrainian society, it can feel shameful to talk about this, because there will always be someone whose situation is much worse. Through this song, I wanted to get rid of that feeling of shame and give myself permission to talk about my own pain. About the desire to get rid of it, at least for a while. At that time, I started having thoughts about emigration, which I still sometimes come back to and which makes me feel sad. These thoughts also made me realize how much I value sincere things about my home, and how lost I might feel without it. It’s strange to love your home and still sometimes want to escape from it. “Унісон”, on the other hand, was written out of a desire to cultivate something in opposition to pain and destruction – something humanistic, something I really value. I feel that these are the things that keep me going now: the people close to me, understanding and sincere communication between us. After writing this song, I even allowed myself to fall in love, because I started trying not to run away from emotions – neither the bad ones or the good ones. So yes, both songs are about home for me. About two opposite feelings I have towards it at the same time: I love it with all my heart, but sometimes I also feel deeply tired and hopeless. Maybe home has stopped being just a specific place for me. It is both the pain connected to it and, at the same time, something tender, meaningful, and deeply personal. Your lyrics rarely describe current events directly, yet exhaustion, fear, disappearing traces, confused calendars, sleeplessness and the hope for a quiet night inevitably acquire particular meanings in contemporary Ukraine. Do you consciously leave that space open for the listener? Do you ever feel a responsibility as a Ukrainian artist to address the war explicitly, or can writing about intimacy, abstraction, anxiety and everyday life itself be a way of documenting what it feels like to live through this period? My lyrics are quite abstract because I naturally tend to think in images. And yes, this is my way of documenting my own experience, emotions and states rather than specific events. In general, creativity is more of a monologue for me than a way to communicate something to the outside world. But of course, I’m happy to find people who connect with what I do. I don’t feel a particular responsibility to speak about the war directly, because music is almost the only space where I can let go of any external responsibility and simply be honest with myself. I think journalists and reporters are the ones who directly document the war. While I document what it feels like to live in my reality, where many other parts of life exist alongside the war. If you had to build a small cultural portrait of Ukraine as it feels to you right now, what would you choose as one book, one film, one song, one album, one play, one artwork, one dish, one building, one monument and one meme — and why those particular choices? This question is difficult for me to answer because I feel like some time must pass before I can look at all of this from the outside. Right now, I still don’t fully understand what Ukraine is today or how I could describe it through specific cultural images. It feels like such a broad and complicated topic. Maybe a few years ago I could have given a more specific answer. But during this time, I have changed, my perception of what is happening has changed, and, as a result, my perception of Ukraine has changed too. So for now, I am still looking for these answers for myself. At the same time, I increasingly feel how unhealthy and distorted our idea of what is “normal” is becoming, while society itself is becoming traumatized. A lot of my attention is focused on this now, and it hurts me. But Ukraine is not only about the war and its consequences. It is also about its authenticity, mentality, landscapes, smells, people, and many other things that are difficult to fit into a single portrait. Maybe that is why I’m not ready yet to choose just one symbol for each of these categories.   SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 – SUMY Kateryna Pavlovska Having previously covered the Sumy-based label Bondeni, Pavlovska is a familiar name to readers of UFN. Her first solo release provides the perfect opportunity to reconnect. Hi Kateryna, “Veselo” is your first solo single after your work as the vocalist of ZzuppamanN and Tvaryny. So, at the same time, I feel completely free. “Veselo” grew out of the news that another friend had been killed, yet the response was not a lament but a profanity-laced, almost absurdly cheerful song—the idea of laughing so as not to cry. And what has changed most profoundly in the way you experience everyday life since February 2022? Yes, in terms of its meaning, “Veselo” is more of a personal song for Ihor, about his losses, although all of us have experienced loss. That’s why he even sings it together with me. But I completely share the emotions and thoughts he put into these songs, so singing about all of this felt completely natural to me. Both songs also contain that very specific kind of humor that has allowed all of us to keep living and creating over the past few years. In fact, the entire label’s creative output is permeated with it, because the creation of most of our songs starts with some kind of inside joke. It’s just done more directly here than, for example, in Tvaryny or Art Sopin. Yes, I’m talking about profanity and distinctly Ukrainian swearing. There was actually a rather sweet moment with “Veselo” when the guys somewhat awkwardly asked whether I was comfortable singing lyrics like that. Apparently, they had forgotten that I had already recited an absolutely catastrophic amount of swearing in ZzuppamanN’s manifesto “Idoly”. After that, everything else seems like child’s play. As for changes in the way I perceive everyday life, I can say just one thing: you start appreciating your family, friends, and creativity more and more, because without them, getting through this kind of “everyday life” is incredibly difficult.   SEPTEMBER 5, 2026 – CHERNIHIV Fedir Tkachov Hi Fedir, it’s been a while! For example, I like live-recorded improvisations because it condenses the aspects of composition and production into this singular realtime process, and by the end of the performance you either got it or not. It’s quite an honest way of making music. Even if I use modern technology to do that, I still have only two hands and a certain level of musical ability. At the same time, I have a relatively conceptual album project that I’ve been dragging for years, refining the concept, changing the name, adding and removing music. Just a couple of weeks ago I recorded a piece that feels like a fitting last track for it, but I’m having a hard time to apply the “no overthinking” mindset and workflow to the rest of it, as some compositions are either too complex or carry too much pain. Listening back to pieces such as “Captains’ Quarters”, “Cyber Jungle”, “Daily Triumphs” and “Everything Ends Eventually”, can you hear circumstances from late 2025 entering the music despite your decision not to make the album explicitly about them? Life events and experiences inevitably inform and even bleed into my creative work, that’s a fact. With some compositions it’s quite subtle or almost non-existent, with others it gets very personal. Honestly, I wouldn’t want it any other way. In the age of so called AI and everything becoming increasingly more fake, at least I can say “Based on real events” haha) Back in 2022 you mentioned your cousin Danny as someone who had supported your music long before you were really sharing it publicly and who helped expand your musical tastes. Now that relationship has resurfaced as Thrasher Grace, but the three pieces on the album actually document an earlier period when you had limited equipment, slow computers and much less technical experience: Daniil’s voice becomes the raw material of “Mindstorm”, his eBow guitar generates “Uncertain Times”, and “Meadow” comes from an improvisation involving guitar, a smartphone used as a MIDI keyboard and a Korg controller.
