I feel I can say for both of us that properly releasing this music definitely inspired us to make something new. There’s no knowing what future Thrasher Grace might sound like, but we have plenty of instruments at our disposal, and we both have grown exponentially as musicians over the years, even if in considerably different dimensions. It’s only about us getting serious and doing the work. When we last spoke, you had only recently returned to Chernihiv after being displaced during the siege, and you described not knowing when you left in March 2022 whether you would ever see your home or family again. It’s quite surreal to say this, but in retrospect that time right after the 2022 siege was quite blissful, there was a lot more hope in the air. Things only went downhill from there, but also a lot more nuance and depth about the war and the world has been revealed. These days the city is almost constantly in the air raid mode, and the density and success rate of the attacks seems to be increasing. It’s not a safe place to be. Upcoming winter will most likely be quite bleak, to put it mildly. But regardless if we’ll have water and heat or not, I have enough battery-powered devices to keep creating, at least for a while. In 2022 you were still able to speak about gratitude, remaining functional and building a future for yourself as an artist. Are you still able to think about the future in those terms today, and has living in Chernihiv throughout these intervening years changed what you want music — and your life as a musician — to be? It’s hard to choose an appropriate lens for this question, but maybe a few different truths can coexist. It’s not all doom and gloom, after all I was able to keep myself in one piece so far, and even in 2026 I consider myself to be blessed in many ways. But I’m 36 now, and I realise that the likelihood of me seeing 40 is quite low. I try to keep a positive outlook on life, but I live a day at the time, and any kind of future planning feels naive and futile. Considering the current trajectory of events, my best hope is making music a little while longer without any big dreams or expectations. At the same time, I appreciate my life’s story for what it is and has been so far, a really nice ride. 2026 was quite a fruitful year for me in terms of releasing music and streaming live performances, and I hope to keep and ramp up the pace going forward. Cello Drones brings you back to the instrument that, as you write, “lured” you into music more than half your life ago. The cello remains very recognisable throughout the six pieces, even as looping allows individual gestures to accumulate into drones and increasingly layered textures. What drew you back to the instrument in this particular way after years of working with synthesizers and electronics? And has your experience with electronic music changed the way you now approach the cello—particularly your sense of duration, repetition and the possibilities contained in the sustained sound of a bowed string? In a way it’s a return to the roots. My acoustic cello journey was interrupted in 2017, when I had a soundtrack project that allowed me to purchase an electric cello, which was a long dream coming true. My acoustic cello was a very cheap soviet factory made instrument, while my NS Design electric is very high-quality in terms of craftsmanship, ergonomics and playability, and overall plug-n-play experience. Shortly after this new purchase my acoustic cello fell apart (maybe out of jealousy?), the back separated from the sides and it became unplayable, and I just accepted that. For years I’ve been trying to change the sound of the electric cello into acoustic with different reverbs, impulse responses of an acoustic cello body, eq, but it was never the same. Then somewhere in summer-autumn of 2024 I decided to have my acoustic cello fixed, and everything clicked into place – both of them became two sides of the same phenomenon, similarly how electric and acoustic guitars perfectly coexist today and there’s no point in trying to convert one into another. The sounds of acoustic and electric cello actually complement each other really well. What drew me back was the sound and the physicality of the experience. I really missed the texture and variety of sonic colours and having to work it, to extract the sounds out of this mysterious wooden box with strings. I still love synths and modular and software, but you have to do a lot of work to make a really emotive synth sound, and with cello you just grab it and play away. I’m certain that years of producing electronic music serve me well now with cello. It’s quite a lo-fi sound, but despite the low quality of the instrument, my self-taught skill level and very close miking technique, I have the ability to make it somewhat pleasant, and to build sonic worlds for other people to connect with on a deeper level, even if initially I make them for myself.   SEPTMBER 10, 2026 – TALLIN Roksana Smirnova and Misha Kalinin You have been working together as a Duo for more than ten years, but you came to it from quite different musical backgrounds: Roksana through classical music and jazz, and Misha through jazz, rock, electronics and experimental music. How did each of you arrive at music in the first place, and how has your musical relationship changed over those ten years? Do you still recognise which ideas belong to one of you, or has the duo developed a language that exists somewhere between the two? Roksana: Music has been part of my life since early childhood and, in a sense, was already woven into my family. My mother and great-aunt played the piano, and my great-grandmother played the violin. I vividly remember my father calling me when I was six and asking, “Would you like to go to music school?” I immediately said yes. It was not a decision my parents made for me—it was my first independent choice connected with music. That was the beginning of my musical journey: first music school, then jazz piano at a music college in Odesa, followed by classical piano at the conservatory. Both traditions played an essential role in shaping me as a musician. In jazz, I have always been drawn to improvisation, freedom, energy, and groove; in classical music, to the richness of form, refinement, and precision. The combination of these qualities has largely shaped my own musical language. Over more than ten years, Misha and I have come a very long way creatively. We did come from different musical worlds, but we have always shared a very similar instinctive understanding of music. Of course, we each bring our own ideas, and at first we can usually recognise where a particular idea came from. But once our ideas meet, they stop existing separately and give rise to something else. I think this is how the language of our duo emerged: it draws on different styles and musical traditions, yet ultimately becomes something new that belongs to both of us. Misha: Yes, our backgrounds are different, although jazz was the common foundation for both of us in the beginning. From there, our paths developed in different directions and we each absorbed very different musical influences. In the end, that diversity has enriched our shared musical language enormously and brought many more colours into it. Over more than ten years of working together, a language of the duo has formed that now exists in its own right. It continues to transform and evolve, but it definitely has its own recognisable characteristics, colours and ways of interacting that feel specific to us. At this point, what matters most is not where an individual idea originated, but what it becomes inside that shared language. Silent Dialogues is conceived almost as a life cycle, beginning with “Inmost Dialogues” and “First Light”, passing through “Night”, “Windsong”, “Time” and “Shadows and Light”, and ending with “Memories”. At the same time, improvisation is fundamental to the way you play together. How much of that larger trajectory existed before you began recording, and how do you reconcile a clearly conceived dramatic arc with the unpredictability of improvisation? What also changed when the Laulasmaa String Quartet entered the music for the final three pieces? Roksana: The music for this album took its final shape during our two-month residency at the Arvo Pärt Centre in Estonia, where we had come specifically to record it. We arrived with a number of musical ideas that still needed to be developed into finished pieces, but as the process unfolded, it became clear what truly belonged on the album, what did not fit within its world, and where entirely new material needed to be created. For example, three pieces: “Time,” “When the War Is Over” and “Memories,” were written entirely during our time there. The idea of the album as a unified cycle also emerged through the process itself. We did not conceive this dramatic arc in advance—the music gradually began to find its own sequence and reveal the album’s internal logic. We do not see a carefully shaped dramatic structure and improvisation as opposites. Each composition has its own form and emotional direction, but within that framework we deliberately leave space for improvisation. It brings vitality, spontaneity, and the sense that something is being created in the here and now. In this way, the overall trajectory remains intact, while the music itself stays alive. Bringing the Laulasmaa String Quartet into the final three pieces significantly expanded the album’s sonic palette. Our musical language remained the same, but the quartet added greater depth, dimension, and new emotional colours. The strings became not simply a background or an additional layer, but another voice in the music dialogue. Misha Kalinin Misha: In earlier years, we tended to work with a larger proportion of written material and perhaps less improvisation. Over time, one of our intentions became to find the right balance between composed music and improvisation – enough structure to shape a piece, but enough openness for every performance to retain flow, freedom and the presence of the actual moment. The larger dramatic trajectory of the album gave us a frame, while improvisation allowed the music inside that frame to remain alive and unpredictable. For us, these two things are not opposites; they can strengthen each other. The Laulasmaa String Quartet enriched the sound in exactly the way we had hoped. We have always loved the colour of a string quartet and wanted to bring that dimension into the project. It also helped us expand the palette of the life cycle we were tracing throughout the album. In the final three pieces, the quartet adds another layer of depth, scale and emotional colour, and we are very happy with how naturally it became part of the duo’s sound. Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Ukrainian artists have had to work in circumstances in which their nationality and the war can become almost unavoidable contexts through which their work is perceived. Do you think Ukrainian artists have any responsibility to address what is happening, or should there be complete freedom not to do so? Looking back over the past four and a half years, are there particular works of music, literature, film, visual art or theatre that you feel have captured some aspect of the experience of this war in a significant way? Roksana: From my own experience, and from what I see in the work of my Ukrainian colleagues, I do not think this is primarily a question of duty or conscious choice. I do not mean that artists have an external obligation to address the war, but rather that it becomes part of their internal creative process. A musician, artist or writer absorbs the reality around them through their own emotions and experiences, and then reflects it in their work. This is how art comes into being. It is therefore difficult to imagine a Ukrainian artist living through this reality whose work would remain completely untouched by it. At the same time, everyone expresses this experience differently. We all perceive life in our own way, so the war can appear in art in many forms – sometimes directly and explicitly, and sometimes through atmosphere, imagery or emotional tone. Over the past four and a half years, an enormous amount of music, literature, film, theatre, visual art and photography has emerged in response to the war. It is genuinely difficult for me to single out particular works, because there are so many of them and each one reflects a different aspect of this experience. Misha: The war has affected both our lives and our work very deeply. For us personally, it became a responsibility to speak about what was happening and to help bring the reality of the war to people outside Ukraine. At the same time, we were very grateful for every opportunity to represent Ukrainian culture through our duo and through our other creative projects across Europe. One important part of that work has been performing our original scores for Ukrainian silent cinema at film festivals in different countries of the European Union and in the United Kingdom. I would not single out one particular work created during the war. What has struck me more is what I have seen happening across the work of many of my colleagues. Again and again, people have gone deeper into their artistic language and revealed something new in themselves. The experience of the war has become an extremely powerful catalyst, bringing different colours, greater intensity and another level of depth into their work. In that sense, it has affected cultural figures both inside Ukraine and those now living abroad. The final section of the album contains “Peace Prelude” and “Postludia When The War Is Over”, titles that inevitably acquire particular weight coming from two Ukrainian musicians during the full-scale invasion. Could you tell us what lies behind these two compositions, and especially the decision to imagine a musical postlude to the war while the war itself is still continuing? Has the meaning of these pieces changed for you since you wrote them? Roksana Smirnova Roksana: “Peace Prelude” was inspired by the first major winter blackout in Ukraine. I remained in constant contact with my family and was deeply worried about them, because the conditions were extremely difficult. Winter days are very short, and many people were living almost entirely in darkness, without heating or even the ability to cook. What struck me most, however, was the way people responded to the situation. They did not lose heart or give up. They remained strong and continued to believe in a better future – in the light at the end of this dark tunnel. This is the hope that “Peace Prelude” expresses: hope for light in both the literal and, above all, the metaphorical sense — the belief that light will inevitably follow darkness. “Postludia When The War Is Over” grew out of an attempt to imagine what we will feel when the war finally ends. What will we feel when the explosions and gunfire fall silent, when we look at our scorched land and realise that it is truly over? Will we celebrate and dance, will we cry, will we begin to reconsider our lives — or will we experience all of these emotions at once? This postlude is therefore not simply an image of victory or a celebratory finale. It is an attempt to hear, in advance, the silence that will follow the war and to imagine the full complexity of emotions that moment will bring. Misha: Both pieces are directly connected to the war. ‘Peace Prelude’ was written by Roksana for string orchestra during a very difficult period when Ukraine was experiencing blackouts. The piece reflects a longing for peace and, at the same time, a belief that sooner or later peace will come – a peace that can bring healing, calm and restoration. “Postludia When The War Is Over” is more contemplative. It imagines the moment after the war has ended. It is almost a narrative from the perspective of an observer who is looking back at everything that has happened – the hardship, the losses, the destruction – from a point at which the war is finally over. For me, it is a kind of silent contemplation of that experience, but at its centre there is also a deep hope and belief that, with time, wounds can heal. To imagine such a postlude while the war is still continuing is, in itself, a way of looking beyond the present moment and holding on to the possibility of an ending, of peace and of healing. The titles inevitably acquire even more weight as the war continues, but the essential meaning of these pieces for me remains connected to that hope. You are both Ukrainian musicians who have spent significant periods living and working elsewhere — including Shanghai and now Berlin. After everything that has happened since 2022, what does being Ukrainian mean to each of you today? Has living outside the country altered your relationship with Ukraine, its culture and your own sense of belonging? Roksana: I think living abroad has actually made us feel our connection to Ukrainian culture more strongly, especially when we lived in Shanghai. When you live in a very different culture, you begin to feel your own roots much more clearly. A good example is “Whispers” from our first album. The piece has a very clear Ukrainian melodic character, but we did not plan this at all – it appeared naturally and spontaneously. It was interesting to see how our own culture came through in our music while we were living so far away from it. Of course, living in other countries also brings new colours and influences into our lives and our music. But our own cultural background remains the foundation. Other influences can become part of it, but the feeling of belonging to Ukrainian culture always stays with us. Misha: Since 2022, my relationship with Ukraine and its culture has become much deeper. The war became a catalyst that pushed us to go further into our own roots and to rediscover Ukrainian culture with even greater attention – its music, its cinema and its broader artistic heritage. Living outside the country has not weakened that connection. In many ways, it has made me more conscious of it. For me, being Ukrainian today means carrying a much stronger awareness of where I come from, of the culture that formed me, and of the value of those roots. The experience of these years has expanded and deepened that sense of belonging. If you were asked to assemble a small cultural portrait of Ukraine as it feels to you right now, what would each of you choose as one book, one film, one song, one album, one play, one artwork, one dish, one building, one monument and one meme? They don’t have to be canonical choices: I’m interested in what that particular combination might reveal about the Ukraine you carry with you today. Roksana: I find it difficult to think in terms of individual books, films or works of art, because any specific choice would feel too limiting. For me, Ukraine is something I experience through its nature, sounds and smells, through the way people speak, and through the taste of its wonderful fruit and vegetables. I grew up by the sea, so my image of Ukraine includes both the sound of the sea and the steppe, as well as the smell of dry grass and sun-warmed earth in summer. I do not think any single work of art could fully capture this image. So if I were to create a cultural portrait of Ukraine, it would not be a list of ten specific things, but rather a mosaic of sounds, scents, flavours, landscapes and memories. Misha: It is genuinely difficult for me to reduce Ukraine to one choice in every category. Because we are from Odesa, so many of my strongest associations are naturally connected with the city. Rather than force a list of ten cultural references, I would choose two things that feel immediate and essential to me right now. The dish would be Ukrainian borshch. The building would be the Odesa Opera House. They are very different symbols, but together they connect something deeply everyday and familiar with the cultural memory and beauty of the city I come from.   SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 – KYIV photo by Anna Reznik Forma Formanta Could you begin by telling us about your musical background and how Forma Formanta came into being? What music shaped you growing up, when did you begin making music yourself, and how did you arrive at the darkwave and experimental language you use for this project? I’ve been involved with music since childhood. I went to music school, where I studied classical guitar. When I was around 17, I formed a band where we played something somewhere between psychedelic rock, shoegaze, and post-punk. After the band broke up, I started trying to write music on my own, around seven years ago. My introduction to experimental music began, as it often does at a young age, with an interest in the London esoteric underground. After that I just kept digging and listening to a lot of different things, but probably mostly ambient and dark ambient, drone noise, and dark folk. I’d loved things like darkwave, coldwave, post-punk, and synthwave since I was a kid — that kind of music had always been with me. But up to a certain point, I really disliked dealing with rhythmic parts. I preferred working with samples I recorded myself and with synthesizers, without being tied to a linear rhythm. I still have much more material like that, and I associate it with my om nyolc project, which doesn’t have any fixed genre direction, sound, or particular vector. If we’re talking about projects that influenced the sound which later separated into Forma Formanta, then it was discovering Hype Williams, some projects released on Northern Electronics and Posh Isolation, as well as hypnagogic pop / darkwave projects like Plecid and Tollund Men. Eventually I came to realise that what I love most is music that is extremely simple in terms of form and harmony, often with intentionally shitty recording quality. That kind of sound creates a feeling of carelessness, vagueness, and the lightness of dreams, and because the form itself is so simple, it becomes easier to work with different kinds of content within it. Zahid was recorded between Vienna and Kyiv from 2021 to 2025, spanning the period immediately before and after Russia’s full-scale invasion. You describe it as reflecting the loss of a foundation or axis — something that might be called “home” — while also connecting that feeling to a wider state of turbulence and increasing entropy. How did the album and your understanding of “home” change during those four years? Did material begun before February 2022 acquire meanings afterwards that you could never have anticipated? For a year before the war began, I lived in Vienna, where some of the first material that ended up on the album was written. It was an interesting experience, but not the most pleasant one — like almost any experience of emigration, I think. It’s natural to want to return to a sense of familiarity and stability, and generally to somewhere that feels like “your place.” With those expectations, I came back to Kyiv a couple of weeks before the full-scale invasion began. My understanding of “home” hasn’t really changed over that time. What changed is that I stopped trying to recreate it, find it, or get it back, even as a kind of fantasy. Maybe at the beginning some people still thought that things could somehow go back to the way they were, but I think by now everyone understands that there is no “before” to return to. It’s not exactly a new thought. The material written during those years started to contain more motifs of endings, finality, and completion. Not in a pessimistic sense, like everything is over and nothing good will happen anymore, but almost the opposite — as a way of living through it, making space to move further, accepting whatever happens, “learning how to swim.” Of course, this idea of “losing the ground beneath your feet,” both literally and figuratively, has accumulated more and more meaning and intensity over time. But I don’t even want to try to extrapolate what this musical material means to me personally onto the events of the past few years. Those events are too vast and too heavy, and I’m definitely not in a position to comprehend them to any meaningful extent. The liner notes compare remembering home to trying to recall a dream after waking, where details gradually disappear and imagination fills the blank spaces. That process seems embedded in the music itself: raw, muted textures in which simple elegiac melodies emerge briefly and then recede. How did you translate this movement between memory, forgetting and imagination into sound? And how do the album’s titles — from “apparition” and “death will disappear” to “sleep with armors of defeated knights” and “elegy” — fit into that world? If we’re talking about the more technical ways of moving from dream or imagination into a sonic modality, then things like distorting the original signal, using raw drone textures, or burying the vocals in noise until very little is intelligible are all fairly standard tools that have been used by many artists. Maybe the only difference is that I tried to push them into something even rawer, noisier, and more careless than is usually considered acceptable. Apart from that, I used the Soviet TOM 1501 synthesizer on almost every track. It has this very broad and deep string sound which, for me personally, is already associated with something pleasant and forgotten (and no, I don’t mean the usual nostalgia about ice cream costing five kopeeks or anything like that). As for the titles, some of them refer to words or phrases that actually appear in the tracks. They’re not really intelligible to the listener, but it matters to me what is there. The rest can come from images taken directly from dreams, or from invented, absurd combinations of words that are still meant to convey a certain image. For example, one of the tracks that carries many of these motifs of endings and completion, “moon cycle flavor mix,” got its title because I was amused by the World Ice Theory of the Austrian pseudo-scientist Hanns Hörbiger. He had this hypothesis that there had previously been four moons, three of which eventually fell to Earth, each time bringing an era to an end, destroying most living things, and beginning a new age. To this idea of global cycles, endings, and renewals, I added the name of a cigarette I used to really like and with which I have some associations, but which disappeared from sale around eight years ago: Marlboro Flavor Mix. You live in Kyiv. What is everyday life in the city like for you now, after more than four years of full-scale war? How have attacks, air-raid alerts, power disruptions and the cumulative exhaustion of the war affected your daily routines and your ability or desire to make music? At the same time, what continues to make Kyiv a place you want to live in and call home? I don’t think it would be appropriate to talk about my own exhaustion in particular. My daily routine has also remained more or less the same throughout these years. The main difference is probably that I go to concerts and other events much less often now. As for music and creativity, yes, the last two or three years have been more difficult. There’s less desire, and less enjoyment even in simply listening to the things that used to inspire me or in looking for new music. In 2022–23 I still had occasional bursts of energy — new ideas would appear, I started new musical projects together with friends, we even played some kind of post-hardcore for a while. Then, for a number of reasons, all of that gradually faded. Even though I used to love Kyiv incredibly much, it has increasingly become a place where I don’t really want to live anymore. At the moment, I simply don’t have the possibility to move elsewhere. And it’s not even mainly because of the attacks. It has more to do with the terrible transport infrastructure, roadworks that can last for years on a single stretch, ugly development (often illegal) and the destruction of green areas, parks, small public gardens, and historic architecture. The list could go on. Ideally, I think I’d probably prefer to live somewhere more rural not far from Kyiv, or in a city two or three times smaller. At the same time, I still of course consider Kyiv my home, and I hope that at some point the situation will change for the better and it will become a comfortable place to live in again. Has the experience of the past four years changed what being Ukrainian means to you personally? In terms of country, identity, and so on, almost nothing has changed for me over the past four years. I think most of my answers to those questions had already formed during the period when I lived outside Ukraine. I can’t really call myself a patriot. What I understood is simply that this is my place, and I want it to continue existing — with these people and on this territory. The main thing that exists here, and that seems to be gradually disappearing elsewhere, is freedom. Very little is regulated here to any serious extent. You can be who you want to be and do what you want to do. Of course, wartime introduces certain corrections to that, but I don’t think they are fundamental or permanent changes. I think this place quite rightfully fits the word “volnytsia” — and I’m not sure there is really an adequate English equivalent for it. It implies a kind of unruly freedom, a space where people are difficult to govern or contain. I like the fact that it is hard to call us barbarians, but we are definitely not modern Western civilization either. It is a frontier, and on many levels, not only socially or politically. There are certainly things here that are completely surreal and absurd, but at the same time it feels like one of the few places where you can still encounter something genuinely alive and real. Looking at Ukrainian music specifically, are there any albums released since 2022 that have captured the experience of the country particularly meaningfully for you — perhaps expressing something about the war or contemporary Ukrainian life that news reports and political language cannot? To be honest, I can’t point to anything specific — some complete artistic statement that really affected me in that way. Maybe this is partly because, as I mentioned earlier, I generally listen to less new music now, and things don’t affect me as strongly as they used to. In my modest opinion, there were more powerful releases and projects in the period between 2014 and 2021, also against the background of a strengthening Ukrainian identity and the political events surrounding it. Or maybe now there is simply so much happening that I can’t single things out from the general flow anymore. I’m not sure. But I’m very impressed by the overall sense of collective momentum — by the fact that under these conditions people continue doing an enormous amount of work. Experimental music in particular has developed very noticeably; before, it existed much more on the margins compared to more conventional electronic music. I like what Kyivpastrans Records and Erythroleukoplakia are doing, projects like Radio Rukh, 20ft, the regular organisation of experimental events, and the fact that there are teams bringing interesting international artists to Ukraine and organising concerts across the country, such as Obscure Bookings. I also really like the amount of attention being given to rediscovering, archiving, and popularising different kinds of Ukrainian music. Maybe this particular growth of experimental genres and events is itself an attempt to express the chaos people are living through. And perhaps that is exactly the kind of thing that neither a news feed nor political language is capable of conveying. Finally, I’d like to approach that question of Ukrainian identity from a different direction. If you had to choose one book, one album, one play, one film, one song, one monument or building, one dish and one meme that best capture Ukraine for you at this particular moment, what would they be, and why? They can be canonical or completely personal, serious or funny, historical or contemporary — whatever feels most truthful to the Ukraine you know now. This one here forgot… I’m not sure how well I’ll manage to capture this exact moment, but I’ll try. I’ll also try not to choose anything too heavy, since most of my favourite films and albums aren’t exactly cheerful) For a book, I’d choose Taras Prokhasko’s Neprosti. It brings back a sense of the magic in everything that surrounds us here, while enormous armies march past somewhere across Europe. For an album, let it be ВІА Два Два Девять [VIA 229] — Best of the Best. It’s almost literally musical documentary: in “surzhyk”, about everyday situations, about vibe, about people. If I were to step away from the irony, then I’d choose Cukor Bila Smert’ — Manirna Muzyka: beautiful in places, strange in others, unusual, hard to understand, and at times unsettling or even frightening. For a monument or building, the first thing that came to mind was the empty pedestals where statues of Lenin used to stand — now without Lenin, covered in graffiti, drawings, military tags, and so on. For a film, Kira Muratova’s The Asthenic Syndrome. Moments of Silvertones When Russia’s full-scale invasion forced Valentin Silvestrov to leave Kyiv in 2022 at the age of 85, pianist, researcher and curator Evgeny Gromov felt a new urgency to document the composer’s work. Moments of Silvertones, released through the Kyiv Dispatch label founded that same year, spans Silvestrov’s career from the modernist experiments of the 1960s to the lyrical Moments, Bagatelles and Postludium of later decades. For Gromov, the project also addresses a significant gap: much of Silvestrov’s piano music exists in scores but lacks an established performance tradition. “If this is not played now, systematically, insistently,” he argues, “it will remain absent.” The two discs trace a profound shift in Silvestrov’s musical language while revealing continuities beneath it. Early pieces such as Five Pieces, Triad, Elegy and Piano Sonata No. 2 move through astringent modernism, unstable harmonies, extended techniques and sudden eruptions of colour, while already displaying the attention to microstructure that Gromov hears in the later works. The second disc turns towards Silvestrov’s ideas of “meta-music”, postlude and memory: spare, lyrical pieces shaped by resonance, decay and silence rather than conventional development. Heard against the circumstances of war, their apparent simplicity acquires particular force. As Gromov puts it, music becomes “a space of attention, of concentration, even of consolation”.   Kotra ~ Rust Torn spider under the fried dome, Melting his wires into the voice coil. After all, how to convey the feeling of a layered consciousness, the “fragility of reality” in the opera, because the main character constantly travels between worlds in his delusions during interrogations in the Lukyanivka prison… The musical language of the opera is consciously saturated with elements of the “fragile” aesthetics initiated by Berg and Schoenberg. A variety of vocal forms, including combinations of modern academic extended techniques and folk vocals, a wide palette of orchestral sonoristic means, including spectral techniques, and finally electroacoustic sounds and electronic processing of the orchestra and voices in real time, are components that ensured the continuous “variability” of the musical language, the rapid change of the opera’s tebro-texture. “About war”, about struggle, about love, beauty, about our dreams, our no less complex and fragile reality, I seem to continue to speak in the language of “Vyshyvanyi”… Among the sirens. They were musicians before the invasion and everything changed for them. My hometown Kharkiv is under constant attack. My parents are there. Even if it is not always in the news, it is happening every day. I also want to represent our underground music culture. I love the music from Ukraine and the people making it.”   ROSS KHMIL ~ KAILAS SUNRISE live recorded outsider power trance music originaly released as a mix for examine-archive platform   Sasha Chemerov & Hidden Element ~ Все Це Колись Мине [All This Will Pass Someday] The release becomes a quintessential reflection of contemporary surrealism, where uplifting, life-affirming music collides with stark social realist poetry, creating a powerful contrast between hope and the reality of the present. In addition to the original version, the release also includes an instrumental version and a live recording from Hidden Element’s performance at Brave!Factory Festival 2026.   Various Artists 1 ~ The Freya Files A Darkwave Compilation in Support of Ukraine She rides into battle cloaked in dusk and gold. The Freya Files (and its brother release The Odin Files) was never meant to be an easy release. As part of a 37-track project, the compilation faced legal obstacles, political pressure we never expected to encounter in 2026, failed hard drives, lost files, production delays, and repeated setbacks that threatened to stop it from ever reaching the public. It survived because the reason behind it mattered more to us than the obstacles. Rooted in the darkwave, electro, EBM, and industrial underground, The Freya Files brings together female artists whose music moves between beauty and defiance, grief and determination, restraint and force. Each track stands on its own, but every contribution serves the same purpose: supporting Ukraine in its fight for sovereignty, dignity, and survival. The release became a testament to resilience. Every recovered recording, rebuilt session, resolved dispute, and refusal to give in became part of its history. Freya, goddess of war and love and chooser of the fallen, represents those who carry sorrow without allowing it to silence them. These artists transform that sorrow into sound: fierce, radiant, synthetic, and unbroken. Proceeds will support humanitarian and frontline aid efforts in Ukraine. 🜁 For the mourners. 🜂 For the mothers. 🜃 For those who dance among the ruins   an honest fox ~ The Weight Of Empty Cities Part III: Horizon   Volodymyr Tkachov ~ Soundscapes “Soundscapes” Part 1-5 were recorded at home studio in 2001.Equipment used for recording is – Jolana Special (electric guitar) – kids toys – MD-57 microphone – Vega 122c tape recorder – bathroom sink, shower and some bathroom accesories. Note on the hidden part of the cassette booklet says “To my patient family”   Cryptic Chorus ~ And the wheels of war keep creaking This album was recorded in the pauses between combat missions in a real war. That’s why it took so long to record. This album is somewhat different from my previous works — on it, I tried to express more of my emotions and personal experiences. I hope you enjoy it.   corn wave ~ elephant entertainment Reissue of the 2023 release with updated cover art and bonus tracks.   Decorodi ~ Topography   Ніщо ~ Каркоза [СТУС-079] The second album by the band ніщо [nіshcho / nothing], which, as it unfolds, tells the story of a man who is given a second chance at life after committing suicide. He tries to readjust to the realities of the modern world. His attempts prove futile, and in his isolation he gradually loses his mind, becoming convinced that all the horrors of the world around him are manifestations of an emerging new world order. He calls it Каркоза [Carcosa]. In the end, his delusions turn out to be real…   Neroba ~ Pechersk Neroba is not a person. Neroba is the name left behind after the person disappears. People in Ukraine say, “This one is a Neroba,” or “This was done by Neroba” — нероба, literally a slacker, a lazy man. Nobody remembers meeting him. Some say he was responsible for early LAN fileshares in Obolon that no longer exist. Others say Neroba is a local demon inhabiting underpasses, relay cabinets and service corridors beneath the city. Our protagonist, Neroba, was part of Da Sintezatoros!, a duo from the young Kyiv electronic scene of the 90s and among the first groups to introduce experimental techno in independent Ukraine. Later, producing music for TV ads and commercial jingles, and tracks for Ukrainian pop and independent artists, Neroba slowly accumulated a catalogue of works where his name wasn’t prominent. The music on this album was created in his bedroom studio between 2010 and 2020. A blend of boogie, funk, house and disco – 12-bit drums programmed on his beloved Casio RZ-1, alongside the usual suspects: a Roland JV-1080 and a Yamaha DX7, a couple of drum machines and a cheap early-90s Boss SE-50 stereo effects unit. Neroba’s small synth sanctuary translated the mood of the city at a specific hour. The artist currently lives in Kyiv. We are happy to present his debut solo work. This album is by Neroba.   Motorpig ~ We Inherited the Ruins We Inherited the Ruins Things are made slowly. Wood is polished. Surfaces are worn down. Instructions become meaningless. The archive burns. Somewhere beneath it all, the machinery continues to hum. A study in repetition, friction, manual labor, and whatever remains after progress has left the room.   Oleksii Podat ~ We Were Born To Feel Everything A long-form composition knitting sundry paraphernalia of intimate value into a tēla that feels as recognisable as it is unhinged — akin to the stroke of a reliable brush tilting just enough to unveil the mesh of the fabric, only to skid into another aberrant tangle.   Doctor Bugg ~ REM REM – Rapid Eye Movement – is the phase of sleep during which a person dreams. In this state, reality feels fluid, surreal, and dissociated. Doctor Bugg explores REM through fragmented memories, a sense of lost time, and liminality. REM focuses on the instrumental canvas. The composition features percussive electronic sounds and jagged, disorienting textures that intertwine with guitar and processed saxophone recordings. With this release, the artist changes course, moving away from a focus on lyrics. Genre spectrum: industrial electronics, experimental hip hop, spoken word, and improvisation. “Listening is a very personal experience. It’s best to listen to this music without worrying about how it might be perceived by someone else” – prescribes Doctor Bugg.   Alex Malch ~ In a Landscape 5 years ago, in 2021, Alex started writing this album and after multiple unsuccessful attempts to record it I have finally finished the project This album has everything he wanted and needed to say, musically and lyrically, and he don’t intend to release any more solo music.   Vøvk, КАТ ~ Split (Live @ Druk, Kharkiv, 17.05.2026) This live split captures our joint performance by Vøvk and KAT, recorded live on May 17, 2026, at a show in Kharkiv organized by the KAZKA Family community. The release features four tracks: Vøvk presents ‘Sil’ and ‘Leleka’ from last year’s album ‘Litera’, while KAT contributes ‘Lyst’ and ‘Bez Pravyl’ – the latter recorded in Ukrainian for the very first time. For KAT, the evening was particularly meaningful, marking their first live performance in their hometown of Kharkiv in three years. “For years, we wanted to organize a show together with KAT, but for various reasons, it just never happened. When this spontaneous gig in Kharkiv came up, we decided to make the absolute most of it. The idea for the release came together quickly: we felt we had to capture this special day and time together. Especially in one of our absolute favorite cities.” — Vøvk We are releasing this split as a Bandcamp exclusive, available solely for streaming and purchase on the platform. All proceeds from sales will go directly to the ongoing fundraiser by the KAZKA Family community, supporting those who make events like this possible in the first place. “We always love playing alongside our friends in Vøvk, and this show happened completely spontaneously. Even though it was our first time performing in three years, we jumped at the opportunity to capture May ’26 in Kharkiv with this short live split. We want more than just dark memories to remain from these times; we want Kharkiv to stay alive and thriving. Intimate initiatives like this – which was Vøvk’s idea – are simply priceless.” — KAT   Serhii Litinskyi ~ Fernstimmen The musical practice common in the time of Ockeghem and Josquin has disappeared from our present-day musical protocols, in which the listener’s customary connection to music is organized linearly. This is symmetrical to the way in which music, in turn, connects to the listener. Today, it is difficult even to perceive the difference between these two connections, but once there was an enormous distance between them. A singer taking part in the performance of a Josquin Mass presupposed a trajectory of sound that did not lead to the listener, because the figure of the listener did not exist in the church in the first place. Even when members of the congregation were present at the service, the singers were either isolated from them or turned away from them; combined with the church’s powerful reverberant acoustics, this effectively deprived the congregation of the possibility of perceiving the music. If we set aside the liturgical function and the metaphysical dimension of the process, and consider instead the physical and physiological dimension of musical practice, music here returned to itself, existing in a reflexive loop. The sound produced by the singer returned to the singer and shaped a state in which he could produce sound that was even more effective at producing the state in which effective sound could be produced. The circular trajectory of the music enclosed and isolated the musical material. When we encounter Josquin’s music, we immediately register the autonomy and coherence of its sonic construction. In terms of expression, it is alien to the kind of expressivity we habitually describe as a reliance on an outward effect. When we listen to Josquin’s music today, we connect to it asymmetrically. The singers’ voices always seem to come, so to speak, from afar; they do not address us directly. We always listen from the side, in a sense eavesdropping, witnessing the circular trajectory of the music and the effect that sound, through the singer’s body, has upon itself. In working on this piece, I sought to reproduce this ancient circular trajectory of sound. This also determined the insufficiency, and ultimately the inadequacy, of a linear algorithm in which the score is realized in a single act: a direct performance, fixed in a recording and aimed at the listener. I needed to submit to the effect of the sound and, in turn, affect it under the influence of that effect. Having accepted these rules, in the course of realizing the piece in sound I substantially altered and supplemented the performance of the original score with sounds of different origins. In other words, I intervened in its realization by virtually every means through which a composer can directly influence the sonic result—from field recordings to sound samples, to the creation of autonomous musical structures and events within this new sonic environment. These almost always conceal the initial material, making it nearly indistinguishable within the texture of the final sound. Nevertheless, it was precisely this initial impulse, at the origin of the circular trajectory, that determined the character and rhythm in which the spiral of this music unfolds. I am sincerely grateful to all the musicians through whom Fernstimmen—“distant voices”—have come closer.   DJ POPS ~ между частотами The label ERYTHROLEUKOPLAKIA out of Kyiv presents itself in a raw, punky style, but this second album from associate DJ Pops is altogether more considered and delicate than you might be expecting. It’s another one with IDM/braindance irregularity at its core, but it’s definitely got more emphasis on the “dance” side of the equation; so no matter how lopsided the grooves might get, they nonetheless are grooves, and hold the attention and the body locked in. It also, however abstract it gets, feels weirdly un-digital—like constructions of wood, string, rusty metal, tape, and glue, sometimes with little creatures running around inside them. [Bandcamp Daily]   MIXES   VIEWING ROOM (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: The piano has always occupied a peculiar position in contemporary music. It can function as a harmonic instrument, a melodic voice, a percussive object, or simply as a source of resonance and noise. In recent years, the felt piano has increasingly become associated with the latter possibilities: its softened attack and reduced brightness reveal a more intimate and fragile side of the instrument. Intimate Felt Piano, by Mondo Loops, takes this idea as its starting point, but rather than presenting the felt piano as a single predefined aesthetic, it treats it as a collection of textures that can be shaped by the player. The instrument is based on a double-felted Kawai KU3B upright piano, sampled across 88 keys with three velocity layers, pedal-up and pedal-down sampling, and up to four round robins. It is designed around a close, warm sound rather than the polished projection of a concert grand.  That choice immediately defines its character. An intimate piano The first impression suggested by Intimate Felt Piano is one of physical proximity. The instrument does not attempt to recreate the experience of hearing a piano from the back of a concert hall. Instead, it places the listener much closer to the mechanism. This is particularly evident in the way Mondo Loops treats the noises surrounding the notes. Felt noise, pedal release, hammer release, and room/player noise are all independently controllable. These elements could easily have been treated as unwanted artefacts of the recording process. Here, they are deliberately exposed as part of the instrument’s sonic vocabulary.  It is an important distinction. The noises of a piano are normally something that a sample library tries to reproduce convincingly while keeping them subordinate to the musical note. Intimate Felt Piano instead allows the user to decide how prominent those sounds should become. As a result, the instrument can move beyond the traditional idea of a piano library and towards something closer to a playable sound-design tool. Three ways of hearing the same instrument The library is organised around three sample sets: Felt, Tape and Mute. The Felt layer represents the most direct interpretation of the instrument: a double-felted upright with a soft and restrained response. Tape takes the concept somewhere else. The material is recorded to tape, slowed slightly and retuned, creating a denser and more nostalgic character. Rather than simply adding tape processing to an otherwise conventional piano, this approach makes the altered recording itself part of the instrument’s identity.  Mute is perhaps the most conceptually different of the three. The strings are physically muted, producing a tighter and more percussive response. Together, these three approaches make the instrument considerably more flexible than its name might initially suggest. They can be understood almost as three different perspectives on the same object: the piano as an acoustic instrument, the piano as a degraded recording, and the piano as a percussive mechanism. The sound between the notes The most interesting aspect of Intimate Felt Piano may not actually be the piano itself. It is what happens between the notes. The interface provides controls for Felt, Hammers, Pedal, Noise and Round Robin behaviour, alongside independent controls for the Room, Ribbon, stereo Pair and Pad elements. The microphone setup includes stereo condenser, ribbon and room perspectives.  This gives the user considerable control over the perceived distance and physicality of the instrument. A close microphone can make a sparse melody feel almost tactile. Increasing the room component can turn the same material into something more atmospheric. Mechanical noises can remain almost imperceptible or become an audible layer in their own right. For composers working with sparse material, this is particularly useful. When a piece relies on repetition, sustained tones, or limited harmonic movement, small changes in resonance and articulation can become structurally meaningful. The sound of a pedal being released or a hammer returning to position can provide information that would otherwise be absent from a perfectly clean MIDI performance. The imperfections are therefore not merely imperfections. They become parameters of the composition. From neoclassical to sound design Mondo Loops positions the instrument towards lo-fi, ambient, cinematic, and neoclassical music, and these are certainly natural environments for it. However, its possibilities extend beyond those genres. A felt piano is particularly effective when the distinction between instrument and texture becomes blurred. A simple repeated figure can be left almost completely dry and intimate, allowing the physical sound of the piano to remain exposed. Alternatively, the Tape or Mute material can become the starting point for further processing: granular synthesis, convolution, filtering, delay, or extensive reverb can transform the piano into something increasingly distant from its acoustic source. This makes Intimate Felt Piano potentially interesting within experimental and electroacoustic workflows as well. Rather than requiring the piano to remain recognisable as a piano, the instrument provides enough raw material to allow that identity to be gradually dismantled. Imperfection and repetition There is also something particularly appropriate about this approach in the context of contemporary minimalist and post-minimalist writing.Repetition inevitably draws attention to details. When the same harmonic or melodic material returns multiple times, the listener begins to notice differences in attack, resonance, noise and spatial perception. A perfectly identical repetition can sound mechanical; a repetition containing small variations can instead suggest the physical passage of time. The combination of multiple velocity layers and up to four round robins helps avoid a completely static repeated performance, while the dedicated noise controls allow the user to decide how much of the physical character of the instrument remains audible.  In this sense, Intimate Felt Piano is not only concerned with making a piano sound softer. It is concerned with making the process of playing the piano audible. A deliberately focused instrument There is a temptation with modern virtual instruments to judge them according to how many sounds they can cover. Intimate Felt Piano takes the opposite approach.It is deliberately specific. This is not a comprehensive piano collection intended to reproduce every possible performance style. Its identity depends on the particular combination of felt, mechanical noise, close recording, and restrained dynamics. That limitation is precisely what gives it character. Instead of attempting to replace a general-purpose piano library, it occupies a much more specific space: the piano as an intimate, imperfect, and malleable sonic object. At $35, Mondo Loops also positions it as an accessible addition for producers and composers who already own a conventional piano library but are looking for a more defined sonic personality. The instrument runs in the free Kontakt Player 8+, so no additional Kontakt purchase is required.  Final Thoughts Intimate Felt Piano is most convincing when considered not simply as another felt piano, but as an exploration of what happens when the secondary sounds of an acoustic instrument become part of the musical material. The soft attack is only the beginning. Felt, hammers, pedals, room ambience, microphone perspective and tape degradation all contribute to an instrument that can occupy several different positions between piano and texture. For contemporary composers, producers and sound designers, this is perhaps its most valuable quality. The piano does not have to remain a transparent vehicle for harmony or melody. It can become an object to be examined, repeated, degraded and reshaped. And sometimes, when the musical material is deliberately minimal, the sound surrounding the note becomes just as important as the note itself. mondo loops product page here’s a demo mede entirely Intimate Felt Piano: Davide Fasiello · Davide Fasiello – broken memoriesThe post Mondo Loops – Intimate Felt Piano: When the Piano Becomes Texture first appeared on Modern Classical Music.

items._cn_summary: 这张采样库专辑以一架双层毡化的立式钢琴为核心，将通常被视为录制杂讯的机械声响——毡噪、踏板释放、琴槌回弹、演奏者噪音——独立暴露为可塑的声学词汇，模糊了乐器采样与声音设计工具之间的界限。整体设计围绕三套采样展开：Felt 是最直接的毡化钢琴质感；Tape 将素材录制至磁带后减速并重新调律，带有怀旧的密度感；Mute 则物理闷制琴弦，产生紧致且偏打击性的响应。三者并非简单效果叠加，而是构成对同一物体三种不同的聆听视角。声音温暖、私密、贴近机械本体，而非追求音乐厅式的投射感。

items.body: Orquídeas em Prosa, the harsh EBM and dark electro project from João Pessoa, Brazil, releases its new single “Lady Death” on September 18, 2026, on Bandcamp. The track marks the project’s expansion into a duo, with Tony joining founder Soturna Cröstä, and features backing vocals from Luiza “Lizard” Marculino. Lady Death by Orquídeas em Prosa ‘Lady Death’ pushes the bass toward German aggrotech Soturna Cröstä handles vocals, synths, drums and bass on “Lady Death”, with Tony credited for the lyrics. The track was recorded, mixed and mastered by Soturna Cröstä at Carmesim HomeStudio, with Luiza “Lizard” Marculino’s backing vocals recorded separately. Orquídeas em Prosa describes the single as pushing the bass further forward than on earlier releases, in the style of German aggrotech, layered under the project’s usual mix of harsh EBM and dark electro. “Lady Death” is also available to stream on Soundcloud. Orquídeas em Prosa’s music continues to explore the darker edges of technological progress through an anarchist, cyberpunk lens, alongside existential crises, warfare and revolution. The project remains entirely self-produced, with Soturna Cröstä handling recording and mixing and cover art supplied by visual artist reptilian.creates. A second single, “Beijo Nuclear”, is scheduled for October 16, 2026. It is currently available to preview on Soundcloud ahead of a wider release. About Orquídeas em Prosa Orquídeas em Prosa is a harsh EBM and dark electro project from João Pessoa, Brazil, started by Soturna Cröstä. The project released its self-titled debut EP on February 3, 2026, a three-track collection recorded solo by Soturna Cröstä at Carmesim Home Studio, with cover art by reptilian_draw. A second EP, “Ilegalismo Electro”, followed on July 17, 2026, again written, performed and produced solely by Soturna Cröstä. For “Lady Death”, Orquídeas em Prosa became a duo with the addition of Tony on lyrics, alongside a guest vocal credit for Luiza “Lizard” Marculino. The project describes its sound as harsh EBM and dark electro filtered through an anarchist, cyberpunk lens, addressing technological progress, existential crises, warfare and revolution, and operates on a DIY basis, self-producing its recordings and artwork. Orquídeas em Prosa is active on Instagram and posts its catalog, including its self-titled EP and “Ilegalismo Electro”, on Bandcamp.
items._cn_summary: Orquídeas em Prosa 来自巴西若昂佩索阿，是一支以严厉电子舞曲与暗黑电子为基调的地下项目，2026年由创始人 Soturna Cröstä 与新加入的 Tony 组成双人组合，并发布单曲《Lady Death》。该曲目由 Cröstä 独立完成人声、合成器、鼓与贝斯的录音与制作，在其惯有的暗黑电子底色上进一步突出低频贝斯线，融入德国 aggrotech 的工业冷感。Luiza "Lizard" Marculino 参与伴唱，封面由视觉艺术家 reptilian.creates 操刀。整体仍延续项目一贯的无政府主义与赛博朋克叙事视角，聚焦技术进步、存在危机、战争与革命等议题，所有制作坚持 DIY 自产模式。下一支单曲《Beijo Nuclear》预计于2026年10月16日发行。

items.body: With a picturesque, pastoral centre, Southern Points reclines towards the warmth of the sunshine. Patient and flexible, the latest release from Greg Baird’s Moss Covered Technology project shelters in the safety – and the surrounding beauty – of the countryside: open fields and cresting hills, kissing gates tucked away behind stone walls and leaves blowing in a breeze of scented blossom. Southern Points (Hibernate) hits all the right notes… Sparse, spacious, and introverted, the ambient soundscapes reflect a period of deep introspection for Baird. Choosing to focus on family life and life at home, there’s something very comforting about the tones here: they’re gentle and approachable, with warm smiles lighting up familiar faces. With the use of a Prophet 12, varying effects pedals, and processed field recordings, the soundscapes stretch out and the flowering melodies melt in the light of a Spring sun. The lightest wind wisps by, and heavier, supporting drones hint at a strengthening of the sunlight as an early morning haze turns to the strong musculature of midday. Scenery is crucial to the record, and its beauty was experienced first-hand. Baird is an eye-witness to the wonder of the day, and he translates this slice of peace into the language of music. It all came from a day out, the scenery and nature around him inspiring the creation of the album. Baird’s photos acted as additional inspiration during the writing and creating process. The organic ambient hues help to turn the original image into music…but it goes at a sedate pace, with everything coming to fruition at just the right time, waiting for the right season. The album is warm – but not boiling. Listeners will still need a gilet and a light outer layer, but it’s indicative of Spring’s welcoming touch. Light electronics scrape against the side of a wooden fence. New shoots rise up from the soil; birds begin to chirp; the evenings are lighter for longer. Bursts of lavender colour the fields. The countryside beckons. www.hibernate.bandcamp.com
items._genre: ambient / pastoral ambient / field recording / drone
items._cn_summary: 这是Greg Baird以Moss Covered Technology名义在Hibernate厂牌下发行的专辑《Southern Points》。整张作品围绕乡村田园意象展开，灵感源自作者一次户外远足的所见所闻——开阔田野、起伏山丘、石墙后的栅栏门、春风中的花叶，这些场景照片在创作过程中持续提供参照。音乐层面使用了Prophet 12合成器、多种效果器以及经过处理的田野录音，构建出稀疏、开阔、内省的氛围音景。旋律如春日花蕾般缓慢绽放，合成器长音与轻盈的电子纹理交织，伴随鸟鸣与风声的环境采样。整体节奏舒缓从容，不追求戏剧性张力，而是强调自然光影变化的细腻层次，将一天的乡间时光转化为可聆听的声音文本。

items.body:
The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了圣多美和普林西比两个非洲小岛在七十至八十年代录制的Puxa舞曲。这些岛屿隶属非洲葡语国家，地理偏狭、人口稀少，却孕育出层次复杂的音乐语言。Puxa融合了来自其他前葡萄牙非洲殖民地的节奏元素，夹杂merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等加勒比与非洲大陆的律动，葡萄牙殖民时期曾试图禁绝Puxa舞蹈但并未成功。专辑展示了多把吉他交织盘旋的织体，主音与和声人声构成旋律骨架，节奏律动绵延悠长，足以支撑整夜的舞蹈。Pedro Lima领衔的乐队以闷音吉他的riff与鼓组对位，Sangazuza则展示了贝斯与键盘退场后鼓与吉他独自推进的催眠感。整体而言，这是非主流地区罕见的文献性汇编，对世界音乐与跨文化律动感兴趣者有独立价值。

items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — A different step in direction for the band after a few line up changes and a period of inactivity, the band came back with a completely different vibe, but with familiar technical speeds and playing. The attempt at moving into a more progressive sound that they tried on Scruillous is more fully felt on this album, with vocalist Rody Walker almost sounding like a different singer, with a cleaner and less punky sound to his voice. At times his range does show some weakness, but the overall passion on this album from him and the rest of the band is very potent. Lyrically being a concept album based on American exceptionalism, it is very well crafted. The track I'd recommend is From The Sky.
items._cn_summary: 专辑经历了阵容变动与沉寂期后回归，乐队在延续技术速奏与复杂演奏的同时，试图向更完整的前卫方向拓展。相较前作《Scurrilous》的初步尝试，这张作品在前卫性表达上更为彻底。主唱Rody Walker的声音处理发生了明显转变，嘶吼与朋克质感减少，整体趋于干净清晰，虽然某些音域的稳定性存在不足，但演唱与乐队的投入度依然饱满。歌词层面以美国例外主义为核心概念，构建了一个完整的故事框架，主题层次经过精心设计。推荐曲目《From the Sky》可作为切入这张专辑的入口。整体而言，这是一张在前卫金属框架内追求转型的作品，在技术与概念层面均有一定深度。

items.body: Review by alainPP — Side 1 opens with "Do What U Will," a surprising electro-gothic track?echoes of Ultravox with vocals reminiscent of Alice Cooper. A welcome return to contemporary rock after a six-year hiatus. "Hey Humanity" returns to a signature sound, with faint traces of Bowie and the Beatles. Colorful keyboards meet a Led Zeppelin-esque vibe?a Xavier trademark?alongside a desire to soar on symphonic elements reminiscent of ELO and sparkling guitar work. A vibrant finale featuring Queen-style guitar?magnificent, yet all too brief. "Driving To Destruction" features percussive piano � la Sheller, staccato drums, and melancholic, U2-esque guitars. It's all here: a dash of XTC and ELO, backing vocals, Supertramp-style piano, Rogue Male-style guitar, and distinctive vocal phrasing. The dynamic lyrics hint at a crash far more serious than it initially appears. "Stay With Me" follows, with vocals melting into a haughty melody amidst a blend of synth pads and keyboards. The lyrics suggest a call to action?rolling up one's sleeves to save Gaia?delivered with a Beatles-esque, crossover sound. Then comes "Charlie Knew," echoing the great Lou Reed; an epic, operatic track with symphonic orchestration. It offers a somber reflection on the times as they descend into darkness, featuring a vintage Bowie vibe and a soaring, lyrical passage that channels Cooper's madness and ELO's hope?a concentrated dose of prog.Side B opens with "Siren In The Storm," an acoustic Western-style ballad played by Kaitlin?a song of being lost amidst the waves. Captivating, narrative vocals tell the story of a siren meant to save the hero; Savannah's moving voice evokes *The Dark Side of the Moon* before a melancholic solo launches "Enigmatic Terminus." That track takes flight with sharp violins, languid vocals, and radiant, U2-style electric guitar. It is a dark, metallic tale of an approaching end, driven by a linear, martial rhythm. "Legend of Mary Jo" is a charismatic track?an old-fashioned tune with an epic, old-world duration. It tells a sad, sordid tale of love in which the heroine stays with her unfaithful husband?a parable for our own disheartened society. Originally written early in his career while playing with The Sun Machine, it is a conceptual piece?reminiscent of the Beatles and Alice Cooper?featuring classical instruments and trumpets. It has a jovial, vibrant feel?I'm sticking with the Sparks-like synth comparison?alongside a colorful, Supertramp-esque saxophone drift and a soaring, Pink Floyd-style atmosphere; a gravelly vocal cuts through a choppy, Yes-style riff and its rock-oriented variations. It boasts a distinctive sound and a solemn finale that evokes the woman's incredible destiny. A track worthy of the prog giants, featuring a blissful, final Mellotron flourish.Phideaux returns, taking his time?true to his fundamental approach. It is an epic journey best experienced in the car?a blend of psychedelic folk and progressive rock that reveals itself to be far more complex and intricate than it initially seems.

items._cn_summary: Phideaux 在六年沉寂后带来双碟长篇专辑《AutoMoto Animus》，延续其标志性的折衷主义路线。专辑以电子哥特质感开场，随即转入色彩斑斓的键盘主导段落，交织披头士的旋律直觉、齐柏林飞艇式的吉他律动与 ELO 的交响流行气质。歌词层面切入环保警示与时代黑暗等议题，音乐上则在古典管弦编制、Mellotron 铺陈与前卫摇滚爆发力之间频繁切换。器乐编配层次丰富，人声演唱兼具民谣叙事性与歌剧式张力，少量女声客串增添戏剧色彩。整体呈现出概念专辑式的连贯叙事与折衷拼贴美学，适合长途驾驶场景反复聆听。

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — This is a mellow, lush-sounding melodic rock instrumental album, with flashes of fusion and ambient textures around the edges. The band deliberately went for a distinctly "human" sound, avoiding excessive editing and resisting the urge to snap everything onto an electronic grid. In an age of compulsive digital perfection, there's something refreshing about leaving a little room for spontaneity?and even imperfection.Overall, this is a meditative album, ideally suited to enjoying while orbiting the Earth on a space station. There are a few moments with a jazz-fusion feel, including a track featuring electric violin, but for the most part the music inhabits its own spacious, melodic world. At times I was reminded of the solo work of Steve Howe and Steve Hackett, along with Robert Fripp, Pink Floyd, and even Pattern-Seeking Animals. But the further I got into Paradigms 2, the less useful those comparisons became. TAP seem to be defining a sound of their own.It's a little less edgy than their first album, Paradigms, but Paradigms 2 is more expansive and refined, with a broader and more varied sonic palette. It feels like a natural progression from TAP's debut, and a welcome addition to the growing body of work from this geographically separated partnership of musicians working across the USA, Canada, and England.The musicians (including several guests) are a treat throughout the album, bringing a diverse range of textures to the music. UK guitarist Suzi James (Fearful Symmetry) delivers flowing solos?sometimes with an Holdsworth-inspired flavour?along with some suitably proggy slide guitar. Texas-based Mark Cook adds the distinctive sound of the Warr guitar, mostly played fretless in the bass role. Together, they provide Paradigms 2 with plenty of instrumental colour without overwhelming its relaxed, atmospheric character.Key to the album's framework and beginnings, though, were the keyboard-based compositions Michael Jobborn sent out to the rest of the band. In a somewhat backwards fashion, the musicians took the pieces from there, massaging and developing them while gradually adding their own layers and contributions. This includes the competent and detailed drum work of Bill Bachman?whose grandfather, incidentally, was involved in the invention of the 33⅓ RPM LP.A couple of the tracks take a while to fully find themselves, including "A Hole in the Ground," although it has become one of my favourites on the album. It also features some surprisingly gentle vocals?a first for the band, although apparently not something they intend to make a regular feature.My one reservation is that Paradigms II could perhaps use a little more grit and sandpapery roughness to stretch its dynamics just a touch further. Whether that comes down to the compositions, recording, mixing, mastering, or some combination of all four, I'm not sure. I certainly can't fault the band for the achievement of putting this together largely as a home-studio project, if I have my facts straight. There's plenty here to admire. "4th Dimensional Wave" and the guitar solo work in "Wishful Solitude" provide a glimpse of what this kind of edge brings to the overall sound, adding even more texture and contrast to this spacious landscape.I can also attest that this album is a grower; the more I listened, the more it revealed itself.Overall: Paradigms II is a thoughtful, atmospheric progression from TAP's debut?an album that rewards relaxed listening and, preferably, a little distance out in Earth's orbit.4.25 out of 5 dog bones- or 4 out of 5 stars for the progarchives system.
